USTR Makes Determinations and Proposes Actions in 14 Section 301 Investigations Relating to Structural Excess Capacity and Production in Manufacturing Sectors myarbrough Wed, 11/25/2026 - 06:19 WASHINGTON – Today, United States Trade Representative Jamieson Greer determined under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 that the acts, policies, and practices of 14 economies relating to structural excess capacity and production in manufacturing sectors are unreasonable and burden or restrict U.S. commerce, and are thus actionable under Section 301(b) of the Trade Act. The Office of the United States Trade Representative (USTR) has also published economy-specific reports that support the determinations. The 14 economies covered by today’s determinations are China, the European Union, Singapore, Switzerland, Indonesia, Malaysia, Cambodia, Thailand, Korea, Vietnam, Taiwan, Bangladesh, Japan, and India. The Trade Representative has not made determinations with respect to Mexico or Norway at this time.  “For decades, many of our trading partners have adopted industrial strategies built on targeting manufacturing, wage and labor suppression, financial and other support, non-market economy inputs, and other market distorting practices that tilt the trade balance in their favor while eroding America’s manufacturing base,” said Ambassador Greer . “In recognition of this, since 2016, leaders ranging from Donald Trump, to Joe Biden, to Xi Jinping, to Emmanuel Macron have recognized the threat that structural excess capacity and production poses for the global economy. But where successive statements at the G7, G20, WTO and other fora have not resulted in change, President Trump is proposing to take action to bring about the elimination of these unfair acts, policies, and practices. In doing so, we can level the playing field for American workers and chart a new, more sustainable course for the world economy.”  For the following 14 economies, the U.S. Trade Representative has determined that certain acts, policies, and practices which create, sustain, or contribute to structural excess capacity and production are unreasonable and burden or restrict U.S. commerce. Bangladesh: Bangladesh’s unreasonable acts, policies, and practices include (1) industrial plans to maintain and expand its manufacturing sector, particularly in key sectors; (2) production incentives to promote production and exports; (3) inadequate labor protections; (4) financial repression policies; and (5) failure to address global excess capacity and production, including through imports and foreign direct investment from non-market economies. These acts, policies, and practices burden or restrict U.S. commerce by (1) reducing commercial opportunities for U.S. producers and exporters in Bangladesh and third-country markets; (2) harming the U.S. economy by contributing to lost production, exports, jobs, and investment in the U.S. manufacturing sector; and (3) increasing U.S. economic security risks, including through reliance on NME inputs. This is especially true in the ready-made garment and apparel sector. Read USTR’s Report here . Cambodia: Cambodia’s unreasonable acts, policies, and practices include (1) industrial policies providing explicit export and manufacturing targets not based on market principles; (2) investment incentives to absorb or expand foreign manufacturing capacity, particularly from non-market economy countries; (3) failure to address global excess capacity and production, including through imports and foreign direct investment from non-market economies; and (4) inadequate labor protections. These acts, policies, and practices burden or restrict U.S. commerce by (1) reducing commercial opportunities for U.S. producers and exporters in Cambodia and third-country markets; (2) harming the U.S. economy by contributing to lost production, exports, jobs, and investment in the U.S. manufacturing sector; and (3) increasing U.S. economic security risks, including through reliance on NME inputs. This is especially true in sectors like apparel, solar, and tires. Read USTR’s Report here . China: China’s unreasonable acts, policies, and practices include (1) long-standing industrial plans and targeting; (2) extensive financial and other support to manufacturers; (3) support to state-owned enterprises on non-commercial terms; (4) extensive forced technology transfer; (5) wide-spread intellectual property theft; (6) inadequate labor protections, including the use of forced labor; (7) lax environmental enforcement; (8) financial repression and currency practices; and (9) encouraging the expansion of capacity and production in third countries. These acts, policies, and practices burden or restrict U.S. commerce by (1) reducing commercial opportunities for U.S. producers and exporters in China and third-country markets; (2) harming the U.S. economy by contributing to lost production, exports, jobs, and investment in U.S. manufacturing, and (3) increasing U.S. economic security risks. This is especially true in the aluminum, automotive, battery, chemical, consumer electronics, glass, machine tool, medical devices, non-ferrous metals, paper, plastics, power equipment, rail, robotics, semiconductors, ship, solar, steel, telecommunications, textiles, tires, and wind sectors. Read USTR’s Report here . European Union: The European Union’s unreasonable acts, policies, and practices include (1) industrial plans to expand manufacturing; (2) policies to promote production and exports with high volumes of export credit; (3) sustained market access barriers; (4) preferential lending through centralized investment banks that target specific manufacturing sectors; and (5) failure to address global excess capacity and production, including through imports and foreign direct investment from non-market economies. These acts, policies, and practices burden or restrict U.S. commerce by (1) reducing commercial opportunities for U.S. producers and exporters to compete in the European Union and third-country markets; (2) harming the U.S. economy by contributing to lost production, exports, jobs, and investment in the U.S. manufacturing sector; and (3) increasing U.S. economic security risks, including through reliance on NME inputs. This is especially true in sectors like automotive, chemicals, and pharmaceuticals.   Read USTR’s Report here . India: India’s unreasonable acts, policies, and practices include (1) industrial plans to expand manufacturing; (2) inadequate labor protections; (3) financial repression policies; (4) sustained market access barriers; and (5) failure to address global excess capacity and production, including through imports and foreign direct investment from non-market economies. These acts, policies, and practices burden or restrict U.S. commerce by (1) reducing commercial opportunities for U.S. producers and exporters in India and third-country markets; (2) harming the U.S. economy by contributing to lost production, exports, jobs, and investment in the U.S. manufacturing sector; and (3) increasing U.S. economic security risks, including through reliance on NME inputs. This is especially true in sectors like health (pharmaceuticals and medical devices), steel, solar, and information and communications technology (ICT).  Read USTR’s Report here . Indonesia: Indonesia’s unreasonable acts, policies, and practices include (1) government industrial policies to promote production and export; (2) inadequate labor laws, conditions, and enforcement; (3) failure to address global excess capacity and production, including through imports and foreign direct investment from non-market economies; (4) financial repression; and (5) sector-specific acts, policies, and practices, such as “downstreaming”. These acts, policies, and practices burden or restrict U.S. commerce by (1) reducing commercial opportunities for U.S. producers and exporters in Indonesia and third country markets; (2) harming the U.S. economy by contributing to lost production, exports, jobs, and investment in the U.S. manufacturing sector; and (3) increasing U.S. economic security risks, including through reliance on NME inputs. This is especially true in sectors like textiles and apparel, mining and metals production, and renewable energy. Read USTR’s Report here . Japan: Japan’s unreasonable acts, policies, and practices include (1) industrial plans and strategies; (2) financial repression; (3) household investment promotion; (4) support for unprofitable firms; (5) inadequate labor protections; (6) financial support for the auto, steel, semiconductor, and optical fiber industries; and (7) failure to address global excess capacity and production, including through imports and foreign direct investment from non-market economies. These acts, policies, and practices burden or restrict U.S. commerce by (1) reducing commercial opportunities for U.S. producers and exporters in Japan and third-country markets, (2) harming the U.S. economy by contributing to lost production, exports, jobs, and investment in the U.S. manufacturing sector, and (3) increasing U.S. economic security risks, including through reliance on NME inputs. This is especially true in sectors like automotive, steel, semiconductors, and optical fiber. Read USTR’s Report here . Republic of Korea: Korea’s unreasonable acts, policies, and practices include (1) industrial and sectoral plans to maintain and expand manufacturing; (2) preferential lending through state-owned banks; and (3) failure to address global excess capacity and production, including through imports and foreign direct investment from non-market economies. These acts, policies, and practices burden or restrict U.S. commerce by (1) reducing commercial opportunities for U.S. producers and exporters in Korea and third-country markets; (2) harming the U.S. economy by contributing to lost production, exports, jobs, and investment in the U.S. manufacturing sector; and (3) increasing U.S. economic security risks, including through reliance on NME inputs. This is especially true in sectors like automotive, semiconductor, and petrochemicals.  Read USTR’s Report here . Malaysia: Malaysia’s unreasonable acts, policies, and practices include (1) industrial and sectoral plans to promote production and exports; (2) preferential capital through national funding vehicles that target manufacturing; (3) failure to address global excess capacity and production, including through imports and foreign direct investment from non-market economies; and (4) inadequate labor protections. These acts, policies, and practices burden or restrict U.S. commerce by (1) reducing commercial opportunities for U.S. producers and exporters in Malaysia and third-country markets; (2) harming the U.S. economy by contributing to lost production, exports, jobs, and investment in the U.S. manufacturing sector; and (3) increasing U.S. economic security risks, including through reliance on NME inputs. This is especially true in sectors like information and communication technology and automotive. Read USTR’s Report here . Singapore: Singapore’s unreasonable acts, policies, and practices include (1) industrial plans; (2) financial repression; (3) savings promotion policies that suppress domestic consumption; (4) inadequate labor protections; (5) financial support for key sectors; and (6) failure to address global excess capacity and production, including through imports and foreign direct investment from non-market economies. These acts, policies, and practices burden or restrict U.S. commerce by (1) reducing commercial opportunities for U.S. producers and exporters in Singapore and third-country markets; (2) harming the U.S. economy by contributing to lost production, exports, jobs, and investment in the U.S. manufacturing sector; and (3) increasing U.S. economic security risks, including through reliance on NME inputs. This is especially true in sectors like electronics and semiconductors, health, and petrochemicals. Read USTR’s Report here . Switzerland: Switzerland’s unreasonable acts, policies, and practices include (1) suppressing the appreciation of its currency below the level that would otherwise prevail under market conditions; (2) supporting its pharmaceutical sector via extensive public investment and fiscal incentives; (3) reducing a major production cost—electricity—for its steel producers; and (4) failure to address global excess capacity and production, including through imports and foreign direct investment from non-market economies. These acts, policies, and practices burden or restrict U.S. commerce by (1) reducing commercial opportunities for U.S. producers and exporters in Switzerland and third-country markets; (2) harming the U.S. economy by contributing to lost production, exports, jobs, and investment in U.S. manufacturing; and (3) increasing U.S. economic security risks, including through reliance on NME inputs. This is especially true in the pharmaceutical, steel, and chemicals sectors. Read USTR’s Report here . Taiwan: Taiwan’s unreasonable acts, policies, and practices include (1) the recurring use of industrial and economic plans to support the manufacturing sector, particularly high-technology manufacturing; (2) legislation that incentivizes and provides support for the architecture of its industrial ecosystem; (3) state-directed and supported research and development; (4) state-directed and industrial clustering to support industry; (5) various financing mechanisms to support industry; (6) failure to address global excess capacity and production, including through imports from non-market economies; (7) practices that equate to financial repression; (8) past purchases of U.S.-sanctioned Russian feedstock; and (9) inadequate protection of labor rights. These acts, policies, and practices burden or restrict U.S. commerce by (1) reducing commercial opportunities for U.S. producers and exporters in Taiwan and third country markets; (2) harming the U.S. economy by contributing to lost production, exports, jobs, and investment in the U.S. manufacturing sector; and (3) increasing U.S. economic security risks, including through reliance on NME inputs. This is especially true in sectors like the electronics, semiconductor, and telecommunications sectors. Read USTR’s Report here . Thailand: Thailand’s unreasonable acts, policies, and practices include (1) industrial and economic plans that target manufacturing and export; (2) sustained market access barriers; (3) preferential lending and other government support to industry; (4) inadequate labor protections; and (5) failure to address global excess capacity and production, including through imports and foreign direct investment from non-market economies. These acts, policies, and practices burden or restrict U.S. commerce by (1) reducing commercial opportunities for U.S. producers and exporters in Thailand and third-country markets; (2) harming the U.S. economy by contributing to lost production, exports, jobs, and investment in the U.S. manufacturing sector; and (3) increasing U.S. economic security risks, including through reliance on NME inputs. This is especially true in the electronics, automobile, machinery, and electrical equipment sectors. Read USTR’s Report here . Vietnam: Vietnam’s unreasonable acts, policies, and practices include (1) government industrial plans and its state planning system; (2) its land planning system; (3) inadequate labor laws, conditions, and enforcement; (4) financial repression; (5) allocation of financial capital to priority sectors; (6) price regulation; (7) encouragement of or failure to address foreign direct investment from other non-market economies; (8) encouragement of or failure to address imports from other non-market economies; (9) encouragement of or failure to address transshipment from other non-market economies; and (10) sector-specific acts, policies, and practices.  These acts, policies, and practices burden or restrict U.S. commerce by (1) reducing commercial opportunities for U.S. producers and exporters in Vietnam and third-country markets; (2) harming the U.S. economy by contributing to lost production, exports, jobs, and investment in the U.S. manufacturing sector; and (3) increasing U.S. economic security risks, including through reliance on other NME inputs. This is especially true in sectors like textiles, apparel, and footwear; shipbuilding; cement; and information and communications technology. Read USTR’s Report here . As a result of these determinations, the U.S. Trade Representative has proposed responsive action in each investigation for public comment. Specifically, the U.S. Trade Representative has proposed additional tariffs on the following investigated economies except for certain products identified in the annexes of the respective Federal Register notices. Bangladesh: The Trade Representative proposes that appropriate action to obtain the elimination of the acts, policies, and practices includes to consider applying tariffs on all goods of Bangladesh of up to 18 percent, net of existing Section 301 tariffs, with exemptions for certain goods. This proposal accounts for duties applied under other, existing Section 301 actions; duties applied under other, existing Section 232 actions; ongoing consultations with Bangladesh on matters at issue in these investigations; and commitments relevant to certain acts, policies, and practices addressed in the Agreement between the United States of American and the People’s Republic of Bangladesh on Reciprocal Trade. Read the pre-publication version of the Federal Register notice here . Cambodia: The Trade Representative proposes that appropriate action to obtain the elimination of the acts, policies, and practices includes to consider applying tariffs on all goods of Cambodia of up to 18 percent, net of existing Section 301 tariffs, with exemptions for certain goods. This proposal accounts for duties applied under other, existing Section 301 actions; duties applied under other, existing Section 232 actions; ongoing consultations with Cambodia on matters at issue in these investigations; and commitments relevant to certain acts, policies, and practices addressed in the Agreement between the United States and Cambodia on Reciprocal Trade. Read the pre-publication version of the Federal Register notice here . China: The Trade Representative proposes appropriate action to obtain the elimination of the acts, policies, and practices includes to consider applying tariffs of up to 20 percent, net of the rate of duty applied to the good under the Section 301 investigation related to the prohibition on the importation of goods produced with forced labor, on goods of China not identified in the annexes to the relevant Federal Register notice and up to 10 percent tariffs on goods identified in Annex A to the Federal Register notice with exemptions for certain goods identified in Annex B to the Federal Register notice. The products in Annex B are products on the U.S. Imports List of the U.S.-China Board of Trade “30-For-30” Lists of Products Recommended for Reduced Tariff Treatment. This proposal accounts for the commitments and 20 percent tariff rate announced as part of the Kuala Lumpur Joint Arrangement reached by President Trump and President Xi on October 30, 2025. Read the pre-publication version of the Federal Register notice here . European Union: The Trade Representative proposes that appropriate action to obtain the elimination of the acts, policies, and practices includes to consider applying on all goods of the EU a tariff rate of 15 percent, net of MFN rates and existing Section 301 tariffs, with exemptions for certain goods. This proposal accounts for duties applied under other, existing Section 301 actions; duties applied under other, existing Section 232 actions; ongoing consultations with the EU on matters at issue in these investigations; and commitments relevant to certain acts, policies, and practices addressed in the United States-European Union Framework Agreement on Reciprocal, Fair, and Balanced Trade. Read the pre-publication version of the Federal Register notice here . India: The Trade Representative proposes that appropriate action to obtain the elimination of the acts, policies, and practices would include applying tariffs of up to 25 percent on all goods of India, net of existing Section 301 tariffs, with exemptions for certain goods. The Trade Representative further proposes to consider whether the additional duties applied should be adjusted to account for, among others, duties applied under other, existing Section 301 actions; duties applied under other, existing Section 232 actions, or were India to reach an Agreement on Reciprocal Trade with the United States that is responsive to the determinations in this investigation into the acts, policies, and practices of India, a tariff rate of 17 percent.  Read the pre-publication version of the Federal Register notice here . Indonesia: The Trade Representative proposes that appropriate action to obtain the elimination of the acts, policies, and practices includes to consider applying tariffs on all goods of Indonesia of up to 18 percent, net of existing Section 301 tariffs, with exemptions for certain goods. This proposal accounts for duties applied under other, existing Section 301 actions; duties applied under other, existing Section 232 actions; ongoing consultations with Indonesia on matters at issue in these investigations; and commitments relevant to certain acts, policies, and practices addressed in the Agreement between the United States and Indonesia on Reciprocal Trade. Read the pre-publication version of the Federal Register notice here . Japan: The Trade Representative proposes that appropriate action to obtain the elimination of the acts, policies, and practices includes to consider applying on all goods of Japan tariffs of up to 15 percent, net of MFN rates and existing Section 301 tariffs, with exemptions for certain products. This proposal accounts for duties applied under other, existing Section 301 actions; duties applied under other, existing Section 232 actions; ongoing consultations with Japan on matters at issue in these investigations; and commitments relevant to certain acts, policies, and practices addressed in the framework agreement between the United States and Japan. Read the pre-publication version of the Federal Register notice here . Republic of Korea: The Trade Representative proposes that appropriate action to obtain the elimination of the acts, policies, and practices includes to consider applying tariffs on all goods of Korea of up to 15 percent, net of MFN rates and existing Section 301 tariffs, with exemptions for certain goods. This proposal accounts for duties applied under other, existing Section 301 actions; duties applied under other, existing Section 232 actions; ongoing consultations with Korea on matters at issue in these investigations; and commitments relevant to certain acts, policies, and practices addressed in the Korea Strategic Trade and Investment Deal. Read the pre-publication version of the Federal Register notice here . Malaysia: The Trade Representative proposes that appropriate action to obtain the elimination of the acts, policies, and practices includes to consider applying tariffs on all goods of Malaysia of up to 18 percent, net of existing Section 301 tariffs, with exemptions for certain goods. This proposal accounts for duties applied under other, existing Section 301 actions; duties applied under other, existing Section 232 actions; ongoing consultations with Malaysia on matters at issue in these investigations; and commitments relevant to certain acts, policies, and practices addressed in the Agreement between the United States and Malaysia on Reciprocal Trade. Read the pre-publication version of the Federal Register notice here . Singapore: The Trade Representative proposes that appropriate action to obtain the elimination of the acts, policies, and practices includes to consider applying tariffs of up to 20 percent, net of existing Section 301 tariffs, on all goods of Singapore, with exemptions for certain goods. The Trade Representative further proposes to consider adjusting the tariff rate applied to each good to 10 percent to account for any commitments in the event that Singapore were to reach an Agreement on Reciprocal Trade with the United States, or conclude other negotiations that are responsive to the determinations in this investigation into the acts, policies, and practices of Singapore. Read the pre-publication version of the Federal Register notice here . Switzerland: The Trade Representative proposes that appropriate action to obtain the elimination of the acts, policies, and practices proposes to consider applying on all goods of Switzerland tariffs of up to 15 percent, net of MFN rates and existing Section 301 tariffs, with exemptions for certain goods. This proposal accounts for duties applied under other, existing Section 301 actions; duties applied under other, existing Section 232 actions; ongoing consultations with Switzerland on matters at issue in these investigations; and commitments relevant to certain acts, policies, and practices addressed in United States-Switzerland-Liechtenstein Framework Agreement on Reciprocal, Fair, and Balanced Trade. This proposal accounts for duties applied under other, existing Section 301 actions; duties applied under other, existing Section 232 actions; ongoing consultations with Taiwan on matters at issue in these investigations; and commitments relevant to certain acts, policies, and practices addressed in the U.S.- Taiwan Agreement on Reciprocal Trade. Read the pre-publication version of the Federal Register notice here . Thailand: The Trade Representative proposes that appropriate action to obtain the elimination of the acts, policies, and practices includes to consider applying tariffs on all goods of Thailand of up to 18 percent, net of existing Section 301 tariffs, with exemptions for certain goods. This proposal accounts for duties applied under other, existing Section 301 actions; duties applied under other, existing Section 232 actions; ongoing consultations with Thailand on matters at issue in these investigations; and commitments relevant to certain acts, policies, and practices addressed in the Framework for an Agreement between the United States and Thailand on Reciprocal Trade. Read the pre-publication version of the Federal Register notice here . Vietnam: The Trade Representative proposes that appropriate action to obtain the elimination of the acts, policies, and practices includes to consider applying tariffs of up to 35 percent, net of existing Section 301 tariffs, on all goods of Vietnam, with exemptions for certain goods. The Trade Representative further proposes to consider whether the additional duties applied should be adjusted to account for, among others, duties applied under other, existing Section 301 actions; duties applied under other, existing Section 232 actions; or the commitments and a tariff rate of 20 percent, were Vietnam to reach an Agreement on Reciprocal Trade with the United States that is responsive to the determinations in this investigation into the acts, policies, and practices of Vietnam. Read the pre-publication version of the Federal Register notice here . To be assured of consideration, interested persons should submit requests to appear at the hearings, along with a summary of testimony by January 5, 2027 . Written comments are due by January 5, 2027 . USTR will hold hearings about the proposed actions in these investigations on January 25, 2027 , continuing as appropriate. Background: Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, as amended (Trade Act), is designed to address unfair foreign practices affecting U.S. commerce. Section 301 may be used to respond to unjustifiable, unreasonable, or discriminatory foreign government practices that burden or restrict U.S. commerce. Under Section 302(b) of the Trade Act, the United States Trade Representative may self-initiate an investigation under Section 301. On March 11, 2026, the United States Trade Representative initiated investigations into the acts, policies, and practices of various economies relating to structural excess capacity and production in manufacturing sectors. The 16 economies subject to these investigations are: China, the European Union, Singapore, Switzerland, Norway, Indonesia, Malaysia, Cambodia, Thailand, Korea, Vietnam, Taiwan, Bangladesh, Mexico, Japan, and India. Pursuant to Section 304(b)(1)(A) of the Trade Act, USTR provided the public and interested persons with opportunities to present their views through a public comment process and through a public hearing. USTR received testimony of nearly 140 witnesses and 1,070 comments in response to the initiation notice and pertaining to all 16 investigated economies. Today, the U.S. Trade Representative determined, in each of 14 investigations, that the acts, policies, and practices of China, the European Union, Singapore, Switzerland, Indonesia, Malaysia, Cambodia, Thailand, Korea, Vietnam, Taiwan, Bangladesh, Japan, and India relating to structural excess capacity and production in manufacturing sectors are unreasonable and burden or restrict U.S. commerce, and are thus actionable under Section 301(b) of the Trade Act. ###

title: 烟幕与幻象——当世界陷入火海之际，特朗普、习近平与普京却作壁上观
source: 中国劳工论坛 China Worker

content: 2026年11月23日 Danny Byrne。ISA 国际政治委员会 特朗普、习近平和普京在深圳亚太经济合作组织（APEC）峰会期间举行了史无前例的三方会谈，恰如其分地为圣诞闹剧（译注：Christmas pantomime 是英国传统的圣诞娱乐剧目，充斥夸张的表演、滑稽情节和闹剧元素。）拉开了序幕。除了满足各自的虚荣心，以及为国内外受众提供几张具有政治宣传价值的照片之外，会谈没有取得任何实质成果。三位领导人及其所领导的政权都深陷困境。他们都有共同的利益，因而合演了这场长达80分钟的政治秀，各自借此转移外界对危机的注意力，并塑造自己不可或缺的形象。 任何人都不应被蒙骗。这并非「大国协调」的开端——事实上，当今所有重大事态的发展都指向截然相反的方向。上周末在土耳其举行了第31届联合国气候变化大会（COP31），这场闹剧的破产收场，更能说明资本主义和帝国主义的真正发展走向。 现实世界正面临种种深刻而迫切的危机，而且这些危机即将急剧恶化，但它们似乎甚至未被列入深圳会晤的议程。一些新闻媒体将这次会晤与1945年的雅尔塔会议（邱吉尔、罗斯福和史太林）相提并论，实在荒谬。如果日后还有人记得这次「伟大」的会晤，历史也只会将其记载为一场可悲的闹剧——世界陷于熊熊烈火之中，三名「强人」却仍在悠然奏乐。 会后发表的四点联合「和平声明」荒谬可笑。这份声明倒也「名副其实」，甚至只字未提与会三名独裁者中有两人目前各自深陷的巨大战争泥潭（而第三人也积极介入了这两场战争）！ 显然，他们也没有谈及人工智能（AI）领域的巨大危机，而美中帝国主义正围绕这一领域展开激烈交锋。就在他们会晤的当天，亚洲AI泡沫加速破裂，股市录得自2020年新冠疫情封锁以来最糟糕的单周表现，而美国恰在此时宣布对中国AI产业实施新的限制措施。 宣传价值 在三人之中，这次会晤的政治宣传价值对习近平最为重要。中共内部的权力斗争仍在持续，其根源在于中国帝国主义国家资本主义模式的深刻危机。在此背景下，习近平迫切需要彰显自己的权势。 在三人的所有官方合照中，习近平都被刻意安排在中央位置。这延续了习近平近期与特朗普两次峰会所带来的政治宣传效应。那两次峰会的内容同样空洞，却让习近平有机会沐浴在中国作为「G2」（两国集团）两大强国之一的光环之下。然而，归根究柢，无论有多少精心安排的照片或粉饰太平的会晤通报，都无法使习近平政权摆脱中国帝国主义所面临的深刻结构性危机。 特朗普与普京的「友谊」 这对普京而言也是一次政治宣传上的胜利。俄罗斯的国内生产总值仅与意大利相若，但其军队规模和化石燃料储量却位居世界前列。这样一个国家竟能跻身世界顶级强国之列，本身就值得注意。这反映出军国主义和对自然资源的争夺在这个新时代所占据的核心地位，与新自由主义全球化时代形成鲜明对比。 特朗普大肆炫耀他与普京的「友谊」，但他对这位俄罗斯独裁者的仰慕早已不是甚么新鲜事。然而，普京能够在谈判桌占有一席之地，其象征意义充分说明了他从特朗普2.0时代华盛顿的「政权更迭」中获益之大。特朗普颠覆了西方帝国主义多年来旨在孤立和削弱俄罗斯帝国主义的政策。随着特朗普在对伊朗战争中遭遇灾难性的惨败，这一政策转向进一步加速，尽管伊朗与俄罗斯和中国均为盟友。 10月美俄达成的柴油协议最生动地体现了这一转变。在油价持续高企所造成的巨大压力下（柴油市场受到的冲击尤其严重），特朗普彻底扭转了美国对俄罗斯的制裁政策。在发动了近五年旨在摧垮莫斯科能源产业的经济战之后，如今特朗普的利益反而在于扶持俄罗斯的能源产业，以缓解他自己在中东发动帝国主义侵略所造成的痛苦！这正是「和平声明」中特朗普最关心的一点：「三国计划增加成品油的生产和供应，以造福所有国家。三国重申维持能源供应稳定的重要性。」 这导致华盛顿与基辅之间的紧张关系再度急剧升温，而乌克兰在战争中势头之所以日益高涨，关键就在于其对俄罗斯炼油厂发动的一系列袭击。毫无疑问，这正是美国不时中断向乌克兰提供至关重要的情报，以及限制乌克兰使用马斯克旗下「星盾」（Starshield）服务的背后原因。 特朗普在「真相社交」上发帖大肆吹嘘他与「朋友」普京的关系，这不仅是再次公然羞辱基辅，也是对美国在欧洲的「盟友」的挑衅，因为他正在与这些盟友在对俄冲突中的利益背道而驰。雪上加霜的是，峰会通报的四点内容中，其中包括斥责那个毫无威慑力的国际刑事法院竟敢指控普京犯下战争罪，这一点显然是送给普京的私人礼物。对中国政权而言，这点也为其在南海争端中对菲律宾（美国的条约盟友）采取的咄咄逼人立场提供了正当性，尽管2016年的国际仲裁裁决已否定了中国的相关领土主张。 美中「釜山停火」即将终结？ 习近平与特朗普之间展现的友好姿态则更具欺骗性。在这些表象背后，两个相互角力的超级大国去年在釜山达成的脆弱「休战协议」已经摇摇欲坠。这一协议曾使特朗普2025年「解放日」后不断升级的关税战暂时缓和下来。 正当习近平在机场铺设红地毯迎接特朗普，甚至与这名战争贩子拥抱，以回报自己此前在华盛顿受到的礼遇之际，美国政府正着手对中国AI产业推出新一轮限制措施。这些措施旨在阻止中国企业使用海外数据中心，借此削弱北京绕过现有先进晶片获取限制的能力。据报，这将直接影响支撑中国多达30% AI产业的算力。 特朗普最初是在其亲信、英伟达（Nvidia）行政总裁黄仁勋被撤职的背景下，被迫采取这一新的升级措施。此前，黄仁勋被揭发与涉嫌为中共特工的黄乐有着密切的商业及私人关系。她本人曾担任一家公司的行政总裁，该公司涉嫌协助北京取得受到出口禁令限制的英伟达晶片，价值至少75亿美元（《The Information》，2026年11月10日）。《纽约时报》报道称：「一个错综复杂的关系网络（其中大部分为间接关系），将黄女士的家族及取得英伟达晶片的企业，与向中国人民解放军供货的中国国有国防承包商联系起来。」 这场危机是引发近期科技股指数急挫的众多因素之一，英伟达的市值较10月的峰值下跌了近50%。中期选举反映出民众对科技业亿万富豪及其数据中心的反对日益强烈，这进一步加剧了危机。 随后，特朗普政府在如何严格执行对华晶片制裁的问题上存在严重分歧，政策再次出现180度转向。在「美国政府高层的介入」下，英伟达恢复了黄仁勋的职务。这凸显了英伟达在科技产业乃至整个美国经济中的核心地位。由黄仁勋完全掌控的英伟达一直是支撑股市的中流砥柱，甚至实际上充当了其他科技企业的银行。 除了发表声明谴责华盛顿的「经济胁迫」之外，中国尚未对最新的限制措施作出实质回应。中共政权与美国一样，不惜押上全部筹码参与AI竞赛，无疑担心反制措施会引发自身科技泡沫更剧烈的崩溃。出于同样的原因，中国及其他几个东亚国家政府近期推出了自2008年金融危机以来，部分规模最大的股市救市措施。 核不扩散的烟幕弹 特朗普荒谬地试图将这次峰会吹捧为历史性的成功，其说辞大多围绕着「和平声明」第四条中含糊其辞的表述：「三国将就降低核风险和防止核扩散展开对话。」 这一很可能本身就是「中国制造」的措辞，与现实完全背道而驰。同样荒谬的是，中共政权的马屁精正热衷于广泛传播习近平的一句话，声称核武器应当被「全面禁止和彻底销毁」！这类言论的可信程度，与北京偶尔挂在嘴边的「社会主义」不相上下。事实上，中国帝国主义正在进行历史上速度最快的核武扩张之一。自2019年以来，其核弹头库存已由约200枚增至600枚，达到原来的三倍，并已制定计划，到2030年增至1,000枚，2035年增至1,500枚。 这给美帝国主义带来了重大难题，其战略规划者不得不面对一种理论上的可能性：同时与俄罗斯和中国爆发核战争，而这两国的核武库规模均足以与美国匹敌。中国帝国主义者肯定会为这样的前景而暗自窃喜：在其主要对手的直接配合下，既能大规模扩充核武库，又能以防止核扩散的倡导者自居！ 为了国际工人阶级的斗争以终结帝国主义冲突 当然，不能排除帝国主义列强在特定时刻达成临时安排、休战协议及其他协定的可能性。这可以包括采取一些措施，对AI的发展或其在军事系统中的应用等实施某种正式规管。然而，世界局势的总体发展趋势却恰恰指向相反的方向。 帝国主义冲突日益加剧的趋势，其根源并不在于个别政治人物，而在于资本主义制度的根本危机和矛盾。这一趋势将带来灾难性的后果，表现为战争、气候崩溃和广大群众的日益贫困化。唯一能够决定性地遏止这一趋势的社会力量，就是国际工人阶级，因为其存在及根本利益本质上都是国际性的。 这种国际性必须转化为国际性的力量、斗争和组织。本文撰写之际，欧洲及世界其他地区发生的事件，彰显了斗争日益国际化的趋势。而开辟另一条发展道路的希望，正是建立在这一趋势之上。必须以国际社会主义改造为基础，提出革命性地反对一切帝国主义的纲领，以此引领未来的斗争。国际社会主义道路（ISA）正是在国际层面开展组织工作，为实现这一目标而奋斗。 這篇文章 烟幕与幻象——当世界陷入火海之际，特朗普、习近平与普京却作壁上观 最早出現於 中国劳工论坛 China Worker 。

title: Media reaction: Who is to blame for COP31 ‘failure’?

content:
打印文章 分享文章内容 展开菜单 关闭 COP31 发生了什么？对总统职位的反应是什么？石油资源丰富的国家的角色是如何描述的？发达国家的角色是如何描绘的？发展中国家的作用是如何描述的？中国的角色是如何描绘的？这对于共识进程和改革意味着什么？ COP31能否发出“积极信号”？上周末，COP31 戏剧性地结束，多个国家联盟拒绝了拟议的“安塔利亚协议”，理由是该协议未提及化石燃料。紧张的最后时刻和缺乏备受期待的“协议”引发了世界各地媒体的广泛报道。许多评论家纷纷将 COP31 的结果称为“失败”，质疑这对联合国气候进程的未来和“分裂的世界”意味着什么。 COP31 报道 COP31：安塔利亚联合国气候谈判达成的主要成果 CB Live：Carbon Brief 记者讨论 COP31 的关键成果 COP31：安塔利亚联合国气候谈判中粮食、森林、海洋和自然的主要成果 COP31：Ed Miliband 如何回答 Carbon Brief 读者的问题 分析：随着各国在 COP31 上举行会议，气候融资承诺下降了 70% 分析：哪些国家派出了最多的代表参加 COP31？问与答：贝伦-安塔利亚的“公正过渡”机制是什么？
互动：追踪 COP31 气候峰会上的谈判文本 互动：谁在 COP31 气候变化峰会上想要什么 人们一直在互相指责，一些媒体将 COP31 的“崩溃”归咎于“石油资源丰富的国家”，而另一些媒体则指责欧洲“不愿”提供更多气候资金。虽然说 COP31 上“没有达成一致”的说法并不准确，但媒体的反应表明了分歧的复杂性。安塔利亚会议上展示的观点。在这篇文章中，Carbon Brief 汇集了世界各地媒体的反应，展示了对 COP31 结果反应的多样性。 COP31 发生了什么？对总统职位的反应是什么？石油资源丰富的国家的角色是如何描述的？发达国家的角色是如何描绘的？发展中国家的作用是如何描述的？中国的角色是如何描绘的？这对于共识进程和改革意味着什么？ COP31能否发出“积极信号”？ COP31 发生了什么？ COP31 结束时未能就土耳其和澳大利亚轮值主席国推动的拟议“安塔利亚协定”达成一致。最终文本被包括欧盟、英国和一些气候脆弱国家在内的至少 32 个国家否决，谈判拖延了两天，场面一片混乱。 《爱尔兰时报》的一篇社论称，这一结果是“在没有达成任何协议或前进路线图的情况下，缔约方会议以前所未有的方式结束”。
这种观点虽然在媒体上普遍表达，但却是不正确的。 正如资深“COP观察者”在CB Connect上的一篇文章中解释的那样，尽管总统的“掩护决定”失败了，但峰会就许多决定达成了一致。在谈到拒绝封面决定时，墨尔本大学气候研究人员杰奎琳·皮尔教授和凯瑟琳·鲍文教授在对话中写道，“这些文本一直是正式谈判过程的附加内容”。 .cb-membership-banner.alignfull { 框大小：边框框；宽度：var(--宽度--响应式--容器，计算(100% - 32px));边距：夹紧（24px，4vw，48px）自动；填充：20px 夹（16px、4vw、56px）；边框半径：5px；背景：

COP31 came to a dramatic close last weekend when a coalition of nations rejected the proposed “Antalya pact”, citing its failure to mention fossil fuels. The tense final moments and lack of a much-anticipated “pact” have sparked extensive media coverage around the world. Many commentators have rushed to label the COP31 outcome a “ failure ”, questioning what it means for the future of the UN climate process and a “ divided world ”. Interactive: Tracking negotiating texts at the COP31 climate summit Interactive: Who wants what at the COP31 climate change summit There has been much finger-pointing, with some outlets attributing COP31’s “collapse” to “ oil-rich nations ”, while others blame Europe’s “ reluctance ” to provide more climate finance. While it is not accurate to say there was “ no agreement ” at COP31, the media response demonstrates the complexity of the divergent views on display at the Antalya conference. In this article, Carbon Brief draws together media reactions from around the world to show the diversity of responses to the COP31 outcome. What happened at COP31? What happened at COP31?  COP31 ended without agreement on a proposed “Antalya pact”, which had been pushed by the Turkey-Australia presidency. The final text was rejected by at least 32 countries, including the EU, the UK and some climate-vulnerable countries, in chaotic scenes as the talks overran by two days. An Irish Times editorial said the outcome was an “unprecedented ending of a COP without any agreement or roadmap forward”.  This view, while commonly expressed in the media, is incorrect.  As veteran “COP-watchers” explained for an article on CB Connect , the summit reached agreement on many decisions, even though the presidency’s “cover decision” failed.  Referring to the rejection of the cover decision, Melbourne University climate researchers Prof Jacqueline Peel and Prof Kathryn Bowen wrote in the Conversation that “these texts have always been add-ons to the formal negotiation process”. .cb-membership-banner.alignfull { box-sizing: border-box; What has the reaction to the presidency been?  In the aftermath of COP31, commentators have critiqued decisions made by the presidency. An editorial in the Hindu noted that “usually, cover texts evolve as a final synthesis of deliberations”, but said the COP31 leadership “thought it fit to push for a cover text early in the proceedings”.  Australian “president of negotiations” Chris Bowen has also faced criticism over how he managed competing interests at the summit. An editorial in the climate-sceptic Australian said: “One thing is clear: Chris Bowen, who presided over Australia’s $150m investment in the conference, has some explaining to do. International reporting has raised questions about Australia and Turkey, the two nations that co-hosted the summit. Similarly, climate-sceptic journalist Graham Lloyd wrote in the Australian that “globally, Bowen has embarrassed himself and diminished Australia’s reputation”.  For Australian news outlet Crikey , journalist Royce Kurmelovs said that Bowen “tried to run the world’s climate talks the way Labor [Australia’s ruling party] runs climate policy at home: quiet, pragmatic and without mentioning fossil fuels”, adding that “in Turkey, it didn’t work”. A commentary by journalist Xu Luyi in Chinese financial news outlet Caixin said that future COP presidencies should “distinguish achievable implementation measures from ambitions that lack a coalition capable of delivering them”. Separately, an editorial in the National – a UAE state-owned English-language daily newspaper – said “the next UN secretary general needs to restore the art of diplomacy”.  How has the role of oil-rich nations been portrayed?  In media coverage, much of the blame for the perceived failure of COP31 has been placed on oil-producing nations – particularly with the final cover decision draft containing no mention of fossil fuels.  Even before the summit had finished, Panama’s minister of environment Juan Carlos Navarro warned that the COP process was being “held hostage by the petroleum mafia”. After the talks had closed without a deal on the Antalya pact, a Guardian editorial said that responsibility lay with “petrostates resisting a transition away from fossil fuels”, along with a lack of climate finance . The “fossil-fuel backsliding” was being led by a “Saudi-Russian coalition”, it said. A Bloomberg editorial also noted that the omission of fossil fuels from the decision text came “amid pressure from Russia, Saudi Arabia and other fossil fuel producers”. A Times editorial described oil-rich nations, “led by Saudi Arabia”, as the “culprits” for the lack of an agreement, because they “insisted on dropping a reference to phasing out hydrocarbons”. In the i newspaper , David Shukman, a former BBC News science editor, described a “deception” at the “heart” of the COP process: “This pattern of lobbying by oil-rich nations has become increasingly blatant and aggressive over more than three decades.” Despite signing up to the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) at the 1992 Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro, the participation of the “oil-rich minority” has been “in name only”, wrote Shukman: “At more than a dozen of the UN’s giant conferences, I’ve seen for myself the tactics of trench warfare and how well they’ve worked. It’s why fossil fuels remain so dominant and why the climate is turning so hostile.” Writing for the Guardian , University College London’s Prof Bill McGuire warned that the COP process had been “deeply compromised” by the “major fossil-fuel producers”. For Al Jazeera , York University’s Prof Ilan Kapoor added that “fossil-fuel power operates well beyond the conference hall”. ( Reuters reported that, according to negotiators from Europe, small-island states, Latin America, Asia and Africa, Saudi officials had “regular access” to the summit’s presidents, “allowing them disproportionate influence”.) In Australian outlet Inside Story , the University of Sheffield’s Prof Michael Jacobs wrote that since “transitioning away from fossil fuels” language was included in COP28 , fossil-fuel producers “have been determined to ensure the phrase would never be used again”.  Nick O’Malley, national environment and climate editor for the Sydney Morning Herald , noted: “The tension between the action the world knows it must take on climate change and that which a handful of oil-rich nations will allow it to take has been growing for years.” At the summit itself, shortly after rejecting the cover decision on behalf of the EU, Irish environment minister Darragh O’Brien told Agence France-Presse that the talks had been “hijacked by some oil states”.  The Backchannel substack collated reactions from negotiators and observers. Among them, Dr Mary Robinson – former president of Ireland – warned of the “disturbing politicised attacks on [climate] science from those still clinging to fossil fuels and looking to sabotage climate action”. In contrast, an editorial in the National loosely described a failure of the talks to “bridge divisions over fossil-fuel language, carbon capture and adaptation finance in the final draft”. It added: “Unfortunately, the gap between countries – major emitters, energy producers and the more vulnerable nations demanding accessible funding – proved too wide to close.” How has the role of developed nations been portrayed?  Much of the commentary about developed countries’ role at COP31 focused on the EU and the UK blocking the final “Antalya pact”, due to its lack of language about fossil fuels. A cover-decision text without such language was “vehemently opposed by dozens of countries, including the EU delegation strongly led by [Irish] minister for climate Darragh O’Brien”, according to the Irish Times .  Similarly, an editorial in the UK’s Times concluded that “several countries, including the UK, rejected a draft omitting the not insignificant matter of winding down fossil-fuel use”. Peter Prengaman, climate news director for the Associated Press , wrote that the EU and its allies “were no longer willing” to leave out fossil-fuel language. (He noted that “top polluter” the US was not present at the summit.) Other media outlets took a more balanced approach to the role of developed nations at COP31. A Guardian editorial concluded:  “European governments’ objection to fossil-fuel backsliding by a Saudi-Russian coalition was right, but they were wrong to rule out fresh EU funding for developing countries’ climate action.” Reflecting on the need for “funding to help the poorest countries adapt to global warming”, an editorial in Le Monde noted that “the most developed nations have been reluctant to increase their contributions, despite their historic responsibility for CO2 emissions”. An editorial in the Hindu stressed:  “It stands to reason that developed countries, which have committed to providing climate finance in recognition of their historical emissions, make good on past promises to shoulder the cost of the carbon emissions that are responsible for warming.” Writing in US outlet Drilled , reporter Rishika Pardikar noted that “wealthy countries like Japan, the UK and Canada…largely aligned with the EU in opposing support mechanisms for developing countries like long-term finance, adaptation finance and just transition”. Climate campaigner John Gibbons wrote in the Irish Examiner that the EU was “right to reject” carbon capture and storage in the COP31 outcome, but accused O’Brien of “cosplay[ing] at being a progressive climate leader”, despite Ireland’s poor climate record. Many developed countries were not particularly vocal at COP31, and an editorial in Japan’s Yomiuri Shimbun lamented a general “low level of interest in and low priority given to global warming”. The editorial concluded: “It is hoped that Japan will continue to fulfill the practical roles expected of it and contribute to the international community in ways unique to Japan.” How has the role of developing nations been portrayed?  Equity, historical responsibility for climate change and a need for finance have all been portrayed at the centre of developing countries’ positions at COP31. A comment in the Hindu said that “India’s insistence on historical responsibility, climate finance and adaptation belongs at the centre of any credible plan to cut emissions”. It added that India had played a “constructive role” to “provide bridging language” in texts on adaptation and the just transition work programme. Down to Earth noted that “India has referred to historical responsibility in submissions at previous climate summits, but rarely with the emphasis evident” at COP31. Harjeet Singh, strategic adviser to the Fossil Fuel Non-Proliferation Treaty Initiative , told Radio France Internationale that those who criticise India’s opposition to fossil-fuel phaseout “need to acknowledge that there has been a lot of mistrust between India and developed countries”. Other developing countries also held firm, particularly on the issue of finance. Kenya’s the Star said the country had “drawn a firm line” at COP31 and would not “back down until an acceptable deal is secured on climate finance”. The outlet added that the country had “ruled out walking away from the negotiations”. Inter Press Service , a global south-focused news agency, noted that the “deadlock” at the talks leaves COP32 host Ethiopia “to pick up the pieces”. An editorial in the Mexican newspaper La Jornada called the failure to reach consensus “suicidal”, adding: “The conflict is far more complex than a mere opposition between the global north and south, or between hydrocarbon producers and consumers.” Indeed, some developing countries sided with developed countries in blocking the final passage of the Antalya pact.  The Fiji Times reported that Fiji “held the line in the final negotiating rooms”, joining the EU, the UK and several other Pacific countries in “refus[ing] to endorse a weakened compromise that avoided to mention fossil fuels [sic]”. It added: “Yet standing on principle carries heavy practical consequences…COP31’s breakdown is a sobering reminder that, while Fiji must keep fighting in global arenas, its sharpest shield remains regional solidarity and rapid, resilient action at home.” How has the role of China been portrayed? Major Chinese news outlets largely portrayed China as a constructive participant in the COP31 negotiations, a defender of multilateralism and an active advocate for international climate cooperation. State news agency Xinhua reported that “China acted responsibly and advanced the conference process, earning widespread recognition from all parties”. State broadcaster CCTV similarly said that the “international community recognised the positive role China played in addressing climate change”. People’s Daily , the official newspaper of the Communist Party of China, reported that China played a “constructive role” in building consensus and promoting cooperation. It quoted COP31 president Murat Kurum as saying that China was a “key participant” in the multilateral climate process and that its support was “crucial to the summit”. State news agency China News Service said that China demonstrated “ability to act” amid divisions at COP31, highlighting China’s participation in negotiations and initiatives on international cooperation in carbon credits and its climate actions in the global south.  Financial newspaper 21st Century Business Herald said that the Chinese delegation “actively participated in negotiations across all agenda items” and highlighted China’s efforts to advance practical cooperation on climate change.   Three of China’s main state media outlets, Xinhua , CCTV and People’s Daily , covered the COP31 outcome.  Xinhua said that climate multilateralism “moves forward under pressure” as COP31 concluded without a deal. Citing Chinese experts, Shanghai-based outlet the Paper reported that China, the African group and south-east Asian countries were among the parties “willing to accept a compromise [deal] to uphold multilateralism, despite being dissatisfied with the draft text”. CCTV reported that, although COP31 ended without adopting an “outcome document”, this did not mean international climate action had “come to a halt” or that previously agreed climate agreements and international promises would “automatically become invalid”.   State-run newspapers China Daily and the Global Times both published editorials on COP31.  China Daily argued that the COP31 “impasse” underscored the “need to strengthen multilateral cooperation”. It continued that China was “committed to addressing the climate crisis through real action.”  The Global Times editorial, meanwhile, responded to criticism that China was “unwilling to take the lead”. It said: “With its own climate governance arrears unpaid, how can western media expect China to ‘pick up the tab’?” Regarding China’s role at COP31, several western news outlets’ coverage focused on its approach to climate diplomacy, trade and the proposed final agreement.  Ahead of the summit’s conclusion, Reuters cited diplomats and observers in reporting that China’s envoys to COP31 stuck to the country’s “accustomed low-key playbook”.  The Financial Times reported that China used the climate talks to “complain about tariffs on EVs and green energy products”.  On the final day of the summit, the Guardian said that China was among the parties that “did not object to the deal”.  Bloomberg also reported that while Chinese diplomats maintained a “relatively low profile”, its “world-leading” companies featured in China pavilion events.  Bloomberg continued: “At a United Nations climate conference that was low on delivery and high on dysfunction, China’s clean-technology companies showed that some aspects of the green transition are persevering despite geopolitical tensions.” What does this mean for the consensus process and reform?  In the aftermath of COP31, many commentators have called for a reform of the COP process. The European Commission is “drawing up plans to overhaul the UN climate summit process, warning that the current negotiating system risks becoming ineffective because a single country can block an agreement among nearly 200 parties”, according to Euronews .  Many other commentators shared the view that the COP process must be reformed. Marco Lambertini, convenor of the Nature Positive Initiative, said in Reuters : “We must be clear: reform remains essential. COPs are cumbersome, expensive, bureaucratic, environmentally unfriendly and frustratingly slow. The consensus rule – adopted in the climate and nature conferences – allows a handful of countries to dilute ambition in the main plenary deliberations. Too often, fossil fuel and agrochemical lobbies interfere with negotiations and obstruct progress. This must change.” Similarly, York University’s Kapoor said in Al Jazeera that the current system results in “an international forum in which the most reluctant participants can limit what everyone else is allowed to say, let alone do”.  The Associated Press ’ Prengaman wrote that “reforms floated over the years include shortening the conference from its current two weeks, limiting it just to delegates and reducing its overall size”. The Independent ’s climate correspondent, Nick Ferris, said the “collapse” of the talks “represents a shocking nadir in the history of COPs”, adding that “the process requires urgent reform”.  Similarly, Pilita Clark, the Financial Times associate editor and business columnist, said “the disaster that was the climate gathering in Antalya should prompt overdue reform”.  Justin Worland, a senior correspondent at Time , likened this year’s summit to the 2009 COP in Copenhagen. He added: “Following the defeat, negotiators went back to the drawing board and created the architecture that led to the Paris Agreement. Today, there’s another opportunity for reinvention.” (For more on COP reform, see Carbon Brief ’s interviews with 16 experts on the topic.) Could COP31 send a ‘positive signal’?  While many editorials lamented the failure of COP31 to agree on the Antalya pact, there were various articles that highlighted a more positive view.  In the Guardian , Dr Bill Hare , chief executive of Climate Analytics , wrote that COP31 was “a line in the sand moment, a victory for multilateralism as countries stood up to the big fossil fuel producers and said no”. He continued:  “The [cover decision that parties] rejected barely recognised the catastrophic climate emergency we’re facing, let alone signalled a definitive move away from fossil fuels.” Others shared the view that numerous countries rejecting the cover decision due to its failure to mention fossil fuels could be seen as a significant moment of pushback. In an interview in Le Monde , Prof Johan Rockström , director of the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research in Germany, said that it is “better to have this kind of crisis and to do something good with it, rather than having a watered-down agreement”. He added:  “It will have a very positive signal: It means that the world is taking risks seriously. The world is taking science seriously.” An editorial in Bloomberg stated that COP31 should “serve as a call for action”, pushing like-minded governments to continue working together to make progress. It added:  “The outcome at COP31, discouraging as it was, strongly suggests that much of the world remains committed to fighting climate change. More than 100 governments, led by the EU, opposed a final declaration that – amid pressure from Russia, Saudi Arabia and other fossil-fuel producers – omitted any reference to the transition away from fossil fuels.”  In Reuters , columnist Antony Currie wrote that the failure to adopt the cover decision could in fact be “healthy”. Elsewhere, in Inside Story , the University of Sheffield’s Jacobs argued that “this COP’s failure might have been what the world needed”.  Related CB Live: Carbon Brief journalists discuss key COP31 outcomes 24.11.2026 COP31 Antalya COP31: Key outcomes for food, forests, oceans and nature at the UN climate talks in Antalya 24.11.2026 COP31 Antalya COP31: Key outcomes agreed at the UN climate talks in Antalya 23.11.2026 COP31 Antalya Revealed: Russia, Saudi Arabia and Australia are largest CO2 exporters of all time 17.11.2026 Emissions The post Media reaction: Who is to blame for COP31 ‘failure’? appeared first on Carbon Brief .
