DOWNLOAD FULL ISSUE PDF In 2026, Taiwan has demonstrated how it prioritized disaster prevention, management, and preparedness at home and abroad. The “ 2026 Disaster Response and Flood-Season Preparedness ( 115年救災及汛期整備 )” plan, announced by the Ministry of the Interior (內政部, MOI), encouraged cross-agency collaboration, set up projects for emergency supplies and remote communication for isolated areas, and further developed search and rescue capabilities. Additionally, the 2026 Han Kuang exercises in August showcased Taiwan’s increased attention toward a two-level response to disasters: it demonstrated the military’s ability to respond to crises— as well as the capacity of local governments and civilians to adapt—by establishing emergency operations centers, while dealing with a massive slowdown in internet speed . Most notably, the government hosted its annual “ Disaster Prevention Day ” (國家防災日) on the anniversary of the 7.7-scale Jiji Earthquake ( 集集大地震 or 921大地震 ), a 1999 tragedy that left 2400 deceased, 10,000 injured, and 100,000 homeless. This year, the event featured testing of emergency broadcast systems (including cell phones, television, and radio) and technology, as well as the mobilization of almost 200,000 civilian disaster responders, plus 5000 volunteer first responders, for local training. On that same day, President Lai Ching-Te ( 賴清德) met with Taiwan’s diplomatic partners, inaugurating the “ World Alliance for Disaster Management ” ( 世界災害管理聯盟, WADM). He stated that the WADM is the “first intergovernmental organization spearheaded and established by Taiwan in 55 years.” These milestones allow Taiwan to strengthen its relations with the US and European Union (EU), and partner with its diplomatic allies, especially those in the Pacific. Thus, Taiwan can strengthen a network of democratic friendly nations, share information and strategies for disaster management, and ensure civilians’ protection in disaster scenarios. President Lai Ching-Te (center) with representatives from member states of the World Alliance for Disaster Management (WADM) and other governmental observers. (Source: Wikimedia Commons ) Taiwan’s International Cooperation in Disaster Prevention The United States The Trump Administration has avoided acting as a world leader in disaster management. In doing so, it has left a vacuum of authority that has been filled by countries such as the People’s Republic of China (PRC). The 2025 Myanmar earthquake is an example, where the PRC was first in providing monetary aid, and on-the-ground personnel assistance –compared to the late, ad-hoc response of remaining US organizations. This was largely attributed to the United States Agency for International Development’s (USAID) virtual extinction , which otherwise would have taken the reins in providing relief from the West. This trend, however, is contrary to the US’ long history of leadership in the Indo-Pacific. Take, for example, the US’ assistance in the wake of the Boxing Day Tsunami in 2004: the US military provided humanitarian aid, utilizing more than USD 841 million in government funding from USAID, the Department of Agriculture, and the Department of Defense. At the tail end of the Biden Administration, US actors were on call to provide assistance following the 2024 Hualien earthquake. At the grassroots level, donations were directed through fundraising efforts by Taiwanese American civil society organizations . Public Taiwanese collaboration with the US Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) has been limited to superficial signaling, with the sole instance of in-person activity being the invitation of the National Science and Technology Center for Disaster Reduction (國家災害防救科技中心, NCDR) to the 2018 National Level Exercise International Observer Program. While some of Taiwan’s disaster-focused institutions, such as the Taiwan Community Emergency Response Team (臺灣民間自主緊急應變隊, T-CERT), are based on FEMA initiatives, these counterparts are facing opposite fortunes when it comes to government relevancy in their home countries. The American organization is facing top-down pressure as executive calls continue for states to take up the mantle of local emergency response. Recently, though, the US and Taiwan’s disaster management partnerships have found a new level, operating with the help of various US state entities. The Taipei Economic and Cultural Office (TECO) in Miami met in March with the Florida Division of Emergency Management to discuss “collaboration on disaster management and resilience initiatives.” Even in the first year of the Trump Administration, Taiwan itself highlighted its outward viewpoint as the US was turning inward: TECO in Houston donated 350,000 USD to relief efforts in the aftermath of the debilitating 2025 Texas floods. Civil society on both sides are also facilitating funding or garnering support for local and global disaster management initiatives. American NGOs such Spirit of America are helping fund a “ mesh network of communications ” across the island, and a drone training program to boot. Across the Pacific, The Taiwan-Asia Exchange Foundation (台灣亞洲交流基金會, TAEF) is helping facilitate inter-civil society organization (CSO) dialogue and stronger cross-sector partnerships. The non-governmental aspect should especially be emphasized, noting that the actions of some other countries’ NGOs remain firmly influenced by state desires. It goes without saying that Washington understands Taipei’s importance to the US from an economic and geopolitical point of view. Nevertheless, a natural disaster might create the same consequences as a foreign attack , thereby putting critical industries and supply chain nodes at risk. The European Union Taiwan’s relations with the Europe and the EU in particular rest on the the ideals of common democratic values , and is marked in economic terms by the ties between Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC, 台灣積體電路製造公司 ) and the European Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (ESMC). In terms of disaster prevention and civil defense, the European Parliament has recognized Taiwan’s “whole-of-society resilience” initiative in the face of PRC coercion. Additionally, a group of organizations concerned with resilience initiatives—the European Economic and Trade Office in Taiwan (EETO), Forward Alliance (a Taiwanese think tank for civil defense), and Samaritan International (a European-based NGO network)— met in September this year to workshop civilian solutions to disasters in both areas. Lutz Gullner, head of the EETO, called Taiwan “one of the reference points for anything related to natural disasters”, citing their expertise. Diplomatic Allies in the Pacific Taiwan’s allies in the Pacific are already suffering from some of the worst effects of climate change. In response, Taiwan has organized international action pathways: along with the US, Taiwan hosted a Global Cooperation and Training Framework (GCTF) workshop “Disaster Management in the Pacific” in New Zealand, bringing about public-private partnerships from a host of Pacific-facing countries. It also highlighted Taiwan’s technical and logistical capabilities in combatting earthquakes, hurricanes, and floods, and its practices and resources that can be shared across the Indo-Pacific. In Tuvalu, Taiwan worked with the US under the Biden Administration to fund climate response projects . While these initiatives have faded in Trump’s second term , Taiwan can still assume a leading role in organizing similar plurilateral funding projects for its island partners across the Pacific, using its own history and experience of natural disaster recovery as a diplomatic strategy. Challenges to Taiwan’s Growing Role in Disaster Management The PRC pressures Taiwan, limiting its international partnerships in all sectors. In the field of disaster management, this manifests in Beijing having long blocked Taiwan’s full membership in the World Health Organization (WHO). It has also used its network of state-funded, controlled, and affiliated media to advocate for its global leadership role, showing off Chinese progress in “global disaster governance” during International Day for Disaster Reduction on October 13. Furthermore, the PRC’s Belt and Road Initiative (BRI, 一帶一路) features the “ Belt and Road International Cooperation Mechanism for Disaster Risk Reduction and Emergency Management ” ( 一帶一路自然災害防治與緊急管理國際合作機制 ,), which aims to increase investment and good governance measures with regards to combating the risk of disasters in affiliated nations. However, the PRC’s history of humanitarian work has not been consistent, as shown by examples across Asia, and is often tied to its own resource security . China’s disaster help in Southeast Asia has been tinged by conditional questions of South China Sea sovereignty in the case of the Philippines, and for Indonesia , claims of restrained help. China has also failed to fully address domestic disaster relief, such as the cases of flash floods on the Tibet-Nepal border earlier this year. While China did provide emergency supplies and cash assistance to the Nepali government, much more could have been done proactively to mitigate the effects of the disaster, or at least work with authorities to evacuate locals beforehand. Moreover, Beijing concealed the extent of the damage on the Tibetan side. In this regard, inviting the PRC’s assistance in disaster relief is akin to inviting Beijing to pursue initiatives that prioritize the flow of at-risk goods into Chinese hands. Thus, Taiwan can promote its less conditional and more equitable framework for disaster assistance. Policy Recommendations Based on the aforementioned, Taiwan should: 1. Expand the World Alliance for Disaster Management The Ministry of Foreign Affairs (外交部, MOFA) should seek to expand the number of observers and partners of the WADM beyond the likes of the United States, Japan, Poland, and the Philippines. This momentum should be harnessed to gather support from the free world, and counter the pressure of China’s similar organizations, incentivizing non-interventionist support for countries’ disaster preparation. 2. Strengthen Initiatives of Disaster Prevention and Management with the United States Taiwan should invite US federal and local representatives to future iterations of Disaster Prevention Day , to exchange insights and lessons learned in this field. Furthermore, while the 2026 Han Kuang exercises officially featured American observers , these were featured mainly in military components. Taiwanese disaster management personnel should play a role in directly inviting American guests and other willing participants to take part in civilian components, too. Having friendly observers thinking about, and even participating in a whole-of-society Taiwanese response—to include managing severed communication lines, rescuing those in isolated areas, or even an evacuation of the president—by experiencing it firsthand is critical experience that can help the US and others respond most effectively in a time of need. The MOI should seek to work further with FEMA to drum up support, exchange techniques and capabilities, and partner on research initiatives for disaster prevention and management. Organizing collaboration with the National Disaster and Emergency Management University ( NDEMU ) would help both sides strengthen communication and the ability to move populations before disasters strike. Encouraging a reversal of the Trump Administration’s push to minimize national response funding is key for getting their assistance in case of any Taiwan contingency. In this same vein, funding can be delegated to cooperation through civil society organizations, and to joint training of T-CERT with American equivalents and other interested parties. This does not mean, though, that Taiwan should ignore US states’ willingness to cooperate. On a subnational level, Taiwan should locate more places to host private and public events—not just in cities with a TECO Office like San Francisco or Seattle, but also in smaller municipalities across the Pacific, Atlantic, and the Gulf of Mexico. A focus should be placed on liaison activities such as those conducted by the TECO Miami office with the Florida government. Workshops with American locales and further local governments across Asia and the Pacific should highlight Taiwan’s disaster response strengths, and encourage these places to exchange best strategies for preparation and real time response. 3. Seek Further Collaboration with the European Union Given the experience of the EU, Taiwan should seek opportunities for collaboration regarding the use of nuclear power and other energy sources that allow self sufficiency under threatening conditions. It should take advantage of a changing culture around nuclear energy , even if the reasons for this are not expressly from a disaster response point of view. It can also look to co-fund projects within its borders with interested EU partners–expanding the reach of, for example, the National Fire Agency (消防署, NFA), which has sought to expand its assistance into the larger Indo-Pacific region . Additionally, in light of the European Parliament’s language supporting “contingency planning” for Taiwan, MOFA should seek more detailed agreements with the EU (or even willing individual nations such as the Baltic states ). Such agreements could cover a number of functional areas, to include infrastructure reconstruction and food security. 4. Sign MOUs with Pacific Allies Taiwan should sign memoranda of understanding with Pacific research and development-based partners, collaborating with experts who know of specific islands’ vulnerabilities—thereby strengthening Taiwan’s position in the region amid PRC pressure, and further building connections with its diplomatic allies in the region. It can target both academic groups such as the University of Auckland’s Pacific Climate Research Team, as well independent organizations like the Pacific Resilience Partnership . In the same vein, it should look to monitor and get involved in up-to-now bilateral frameworks for tsunami relief, such as in the case of Hawaii and Samoa’s National Disaster Preparedness Baseline Assessment (NDPBA). Conclusion Natural and geopolitical factors compel Taiwan to be ready for disasters. However, Taiwanese people are not isolated from the goodwill of the rest of the world. Given its geography and aforementioned history, Taiwan has the capabilities to become a reliable partner in disaster management around the world. Taiwan should leverage its capabilities and share its expertise, thereby strengthening both its own resilience and its relationships across the democratic world. The main point: Taiwan should further collaborate with the US and the EU with regards to disaster prevention and management, especially utilizing its mastery of subnational and civil society-based diplomacy, while taking a leadership role in disaster preparation and as a research collaborator amongst its diplomatic partners in the Pacific. This outreach will help skirt the challenges it faces in terms of pressure on the global stage. The post Taiwan as a Partner and Leader in Disaster Prevention and Management appeared first on Global Taiwan Institute .

title: In Pictures: Hundreds gather for Catholic memorial mass on eve of Tai Po fire’s first anniversary
zh_title: 图片中：大埔火灾一周年前夕，数百人聚集参加天主教纪念弥撒
summary: 去年大埔致命火灾一周年纪念日前夕，数百人聚集在一起举行天主教弥撒，一名神父称这次仪式是与幸存者的陪伴，并宣读了 168 名遇难者的名字以示悼念。 2026 年 11 月 25 日，一场天主教弥撒纪念大埔火灾受害者。照片：Kyle Lam/HKFP。天主教香港教区周三晚上在中环圣母无染原罪主教座堂举行了追悼弥撒，有200多名死者家属参加。所有168名遇难者的名字都被展示在了现场
content:
去年大埔致命火灾一周年纪念日前夕，数百人聚集在一起举行天主教弥撒，一名神父称这次仪式是与幸存者的陪伴，并宣读了 168 名遇难者的名字以示悼念。 2026 年 11 月 25 日，一场天主教弥撒纪念大埔火灾受害者。照片：Kyle Lam/HKFP。天主教香港教区周三晚上在中环圣母无染原罪主教座堂举行了追悼弥撒，有200多名死者家属参加。所有 168 名遇难者的名字都陈列在圣所的中央，下面还放着一些遇难者的肖像。他们的名字也印在数字礼拜仪式小册子上。 2026 年 11 月 25 日，一场天主教弥撒纪念大埔火灾受害者。照片：Kyle Lam/HKFP。主持仪式的陈华明神父在讲道中表示，这场致命的大火是一次集体创伤，幸存者、他们的家人和公众都遭受了巨大的痛苦和悲伤。陈用粤语说：“追悼会聚集了分散的、独自悲伤的人们，让他们意识到他们并不孤单面对这一切。” 2026 年 11 月 25 日，一场天主教弥撒纪念大埔火灾受害者。照片：Kyle Lam/HKFP。
他还将这场悲剧描述为源于“人为错误和系统性故障”，这与一个独立委员会的调查结果相呼应，该调查将装修承包商和项目顾问列为“罪魁祸首”，并强调了政府监管的失误。“这项服务提醒我们，人的生命不是可随意处置的数字，而是来自上帝的珍贵礼物，”他说。 “这种对生命的坚韧应该转化为对真理和正义的追求。” 2026 年 11 月 25 日，一场天主教弥撒纪念大埔火灾受害者。照片：Kyle Lam/HKFP。香港福音派信义会钻石堂牧师林珍妮在火灾中失去了三名亲戚，她也在弥撒中发表了讲话，当天恰逢她一位已故亲戚的生日。 “但我不能再亲自祝他们生日快乐了，”她用粤语说。林郑月娥表示，过去的一年对死者家属来说充满了挑战，并列举了葬礼安排方面的繁重行政职责以及悲剧造成的情感损失。 2026 年 11 月 25 日，一场天主教弥撒纪念大埔火灾受害者。照片：Kyle Lam/HKFP。她说，虽然时间并没有减轻痛苦，但她祈祷家人能够过上好日子，并保留对亲人的记忆。她补充说，这并不意味着忘记受害者，而是从创伤中治愈，同时为悲伤留出空间。
四名失去亲人的幸存者大声朗读了 168 名遇难者的名字，最后是在与大火搏斗中牺牲的消防员何伟豪。2026 年 11 月 25 日，一场天主教弥撒悼念大埔火灾遇难者。照片：Kyle Lam/HKFP。 2026 年 11 月 25 日，一场天主教弥撒纪念大埔火灾受害者。照片：Kyle Lam/HKFP。宏福苑宏新楼居民大聪在葬礼结束后告诉记者，当受害者的名字被大声念出来时，她感到很安慰，并补充说，死者家属承受着无法用言语形容的痛苦。在大火中失去母亲的菲利斯·罗(Phyllis Lo)表示，当她听到母亲的名字时，她感到很平静，并想象着其他受害者的名字被读出时的生活。 2026 年 11 月 25 日，一场天主教弥撒纪念大埔火灾遇难者。

【原文 English Original】
Hundreds gathered on the eve of the first anniversary of last year’s deadly Tai Po fire for a Catholic mass, where a priest described the service as an act of companionship with survivors and the names of the 168 people who perished were read out in tribute. A Catholic mass remembering Tai Po fire victims on November 25, 2026. Photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP. The Catholic Diocese of Hong Kong held the memorial mass on Wednesday evening at the Cathedral of the Immaculate Conception in Central, with members of bereaved families among more than 200 attendees. The names of all 168 victims were displayed at the centre of the sanctuary, with portraits of some placed underneath. Their names were also printed in digital liturgy booklets. A Catholic mass remembering Tai Po fire victims on November 25, 2026. Photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP. Father Dominic Chan, who presided over the service, said during his homily that the deadly blaze was a collective trauma, and that survivors, their families and members of the public all suffered immense pain and grief. “The memorial mass brings together scattered people who grieve on their own, to make them realise that they are not alone in facing this,” Chan said in Cantonese. A Catholic mass remembering Tai Po fire victims on November 25, 2026. Photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP. He also described the tragedy as one stemming from “human errors and systemic failures,” echoing an independent committee’s findings that named a renovation contractor and project consultant as the “main culprits” and highlighted lapses in government oversight. “This service reminds us that human lives are not disposable numbers, but cherished gifts from God,” he said. “This tenacity for life should be transformed into a pursuit for truth and justice.” A Catholic mass remembering Tai Po fire victims on November 25, 2026. Photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP. Jenny Lam, a pastor at the Diamond Church of the Evangelical Lutheran Church of Hong Kong who lost three relatives in the fire, also spoke during the mass, which coincided with the birthday of one of her late relatives. “But I can no longer wish them happy birthday in person,” she said in Cantonese. The past year had been full of challenges for bereaved families, Lam said, citing the enormous administrative duties surrounding funeral arrangements alongside the emotional toll of the tragedy. A Catholic mass remembering Tai Po fire victims on November 25, 2026. Photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP. While time had not dulled the pain, she said, she prayed that families would be able to live well and keep alive the memories of their loved ones. That did not mean forgetting the victims, but healing from the trauma while allowing room for grief, she added. The names of the 168 victims were read aloud by four bereaved survivors, ending with Ho Wai-ho, a firefighter who died in the line of duty battling the blaze. A Catholic mass remembering Tai Po fire victims on November 25, 2026. Photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP. A Catholic mass remembering Tai Po fire victims on November 25, 2026. Photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP. Da Chung, a resident of Wang Fuk Court’s Wang Sun House, told reporters after the service that she felt solace as the victims’ names were read aloud, adding that bereaved families carry pain that words cannot describe. Phyllis Lo, who lost her mother in the blaze, said she felt calm when she heard her mother’s name, and imagined the lives of the other victims as their names were read out. A Catholic mass remembering Tai Po fire victims on November 25, 2026. Photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP. Wednesday’s mass was overshadowed by controversy surrounding police enquiries into memorial events related to the Tai Po fire earlier this month. One church, the Immaculate Heart of Mary Church in Tai Po , has since replaced its anniversary mass with a general service for “the brothers and sisters who died in the past year.” A Catholic mass remembering Tai Po fire victims on November 25, 2026. Photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP. Parishioners have criticised authorities for exerting pressure, but security chief Chris Tang has defended the move , saying it was necessary for authorities to assess risks for public events. A Catholic mass remembering Tai Po fire victims on November 25, 2026. Photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP. Agnes Ng, a Catholic who lost her mother in the blaze, told HKFP on Wednesday that she had helped organise the mass while residing overseas. She struck a defiant note when asked whether she perceived pressure from the authorities. A Catholic mass remembering Tai Po fire victims on November 25, 2026. Photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP. “They were being oversensitive… The fire occurred in Tai Po, and the Tai Po church was the most appropriate venue for a memorial service,” she said in Cantonese. “If police ask me, I will welcome them.” “[The blaze] is not just a Wang Fuk Court matter. It relates to all Hongkongers,” she added. “It’s sensible, lawful and reasonable for us to hold a mass to honour the dead. Why do we have to self-censor?”

title: 蘇暁康：下一個「民族寓言」誰來寫？
summary: 作者臉書 2026-11-25 【按：深圳的光鮮亮麗，以及它從一個小漁村暴漲至今的發跡史，都是一個「中國敘述史」的簡略版本，它亮麗得太短，因為中國人又懷念起魯迅了，說明她還在「前現代」和農民大國掙扎，也沒有逃出「民族預言」的詛咒，諸如「吃人」、溺婴、婴儿汤、吃药、「中国病毒」⋯⋯。】 一、崛起：全球政治菁英的整體失敗 二〇一九年底，在国际视野里的最大新闻，却是“中国崛起”，其最初信号来自两本英文周刊。 封面上章子怡笑容可掬，背后衬着万里长城和上海东方明珠塔，两件中国的标志性
content: 作者臉書 2026-11-25 【按：深圳的光鮮亮麗，以及它從一個小漁村暴漲至今的發跡史，都是一個「中國敘述史」的簡略版本，它亮麗得太短，因為中國人又懷念起魯迅了，說明她還在「前現代」和農民大國掙扎，也沒有逃出「民族預言」的詛咒，諸如「吃人」、溺婴、婴儿汤、吃药、「中国病毒」⋯⋯。】 一、崛起：全球政治菁英的整體失敗 二〇一九年底，在国际视野里的最大新闻，却是“中国崛起”，其最初信号来自两本英文周刊。 封面上章子怡笑容可掬，背后衬着万里长城和上海东方明珠塔，两件中国的标志性建筑。2005年5月初，最新一期美国《新闻周刊》推出封面故事：中国的世纪 (china’s century )，用21个版面进行密集报道，从商业、教育、电影等多个角度解读当今中国，它明确阐释就是：中国的崛起已不再是预测，而是事实。但是这个特别报道是留有余地的，以“未来是否属于中国？”为总题，因为崛起的含义，只在经济层面。 比如，中国激活世界经济。数字表明，中国一切都很大，有13亿人口，是世界最大的煤、钢铁和水泥生产国，是世界第二大能源消费国和第三大石油进口国，这样一个经济体，为全世界带来了明显和惊人的利益，特别是对于美国，廉价的中国产品，在上个世纪使美国消费者节省了超过6000亿美元，更有一种分析认为，中国经济的强劲增长，使全世界经济免于萧条。 过去四百年年中，全球强权有两个主要变化，第一个是17世纪欧洲的兴起，第二个是19世纪末、20世纪初美国的独大，现在中国与印度的兴起以及日本的持续发展，代表了亚洲的崛起，这是不是意味着欧洲和美国衰落了呢？ https://www.facebook.com/xiaokang.su/posts/10157925323368331 二、從崛起到坍塌 2012年中国正在崛起，难道是比拟纳粹的崛起吗？ 89则是对中共很不祥的数字，自然直指它的执政危机。 但是有人分析： ——中国根本就不可能出希特勒，眼下到处都腐败，就更不可能，出了也让老百姓把他赶下去； ——中国出现的专制，肯定是土的，水平低的，是中国专制主义加一点现代化； ——这个土的，不会是“Hi，希特勒”，也不会是“伟大领袖毛主席万岁”； 显然，有看走眼的成分，也有惊人的准确；其二，似乎曾在中国横行的毛泽东统治，死了几千万人，不叫专制，这是遗忘呢，还是虚无？ 更重要的是第三，还有改革开放吗？改革死了吗？尤其2018年岁尾中共煞有介事高调纪念改革开放40周年，一种“伪改革”还冠冕堂皇地活在主流话语中，企业家、知名党内外知识份子，仍在谈“改革经”。 https://www.facebook.com/xiaokang.su/posts/10161000344588331 三、今天中国的「民族寓言」是什么？ 我过去以为今天的年輕人不認識魯迅，如今網上每每見人喜歡引用名句（現在叫「金句」），是不是魯迅的引用率最高？當然因為魯迅最深刻，不過我覺得恐怕也是他最刻薄——當下人們恨中共恨中國恨習，自然最喜歡最刻薄的名句，像胡適那種不帶火氣的溫吞句是無人理睬的，可能也被引用得最少。不過大夥兒可能忘了，喜歡引用名人名句恰是一種「失語」現象，因為自己忽然有了某種比較深刻的想法，卻一時欠缺用自己的語詞表達出來，看到某個名句正好暢快淋灕地表達了自己想說的，馬上拿來引用。 不过，知道毛澤東的「靈魂深處爆發革命」，源頭在鲁迅那裡的人可能不多。中國因為落後而需要改造人的思想，就跟得病需要吃藥一樣，這是魯迅發明的一種「五四」傳統，最終成為共產黨的一把利器，中宣部及其黨報電視台，至今使喚它得心應手，他們不懂什么「劣等人種」，只有「病人」概念，中国人至今還是阿Q、閏土、華老栓，一代代人都要服药（改造）。 今天人们依然叹服魯迅骂中国人「坐稳了奴隶」的深刻，可是无人询问今天的「民族寓言」是什么？中国不「吃人」了吗？溺婴、婴儿汤算什么？中国人不是还在吃药吗？中国开发病毒「泄漏」到全球，跟当年英国人贩鸦片到中国，是一种因果关系？「大国崛起」的原动力来自当年的「亡国灭种」，这可能是一部新的「民族寓言」？ https://www.facebook.com/xiaokang.su/posts/10160793058903331 https://vocus.cc/article/6b0659edfd89780001cfafb4... vocus.cc APEC鎂光燈外看深圳

title: 刘路：光荣与梦想——我的律师手记（连载十一）下部 为自由辩护 第十章 李元龙煽动颠覆国家政权案
summary: 下部 为自由辩护 在为自由而辩护的道路上，先驱者倒下去，更多的后来者将接过接力棒继续奋勇前行。 ——题记 第十章 李元龙煽动颠覆国家政权案 李元龙，1960年生，贵州《毕节日报》周末特刊部编辑、记者。 2005年9月9日，因涉嫌煽动颠覆国家政权罪被贵州省国家安全厅刑事拘留；9月23日改为监视居住；9月29日被逮捕。 2006年7月12日，毕节地区中级人民法院以煽动颠覆国家政权罪判处其有期徒刑二年，剥夺政治权利二年。二审维持原判。 一 接案 二〇〇五年秋天，贵州毕节的党报记者李
content: 下部 为自由辩护 在为自由而辩护的道路上，先驱者倒下去，更多的后来者将接过接力棒继续奋勇前行。 ——题记 第十章 李元龙煽动颠覆国家政权案 李元龙，1960年生，贵州《毕节日报》周末特刊部编辑、记者。 2005年9月9日，因涉嫌煽动颠覆国家政权罪被贵州省国家安全厅刑事拘留；9月23日改为监视居住；9月29日被逮捕。 2006年7月12日，毕节地区中级人民法院以煽动颠覆国家政权罪判处其有期徒刑二年，剥夺政治权利二年。二审维持原判。 一 接案 二〇〇五年秋天，贵州毕节的党报记者李元龙因为四篇网络文章被国家安全厅抓了，罪名是煽动颠覆国家政权。 被抓之前，没有人知道他。一个西南山区小报的记者，用“夜狼”的笔名在海外网站发了几篇文章，回复不过几十人次。是安全厅抓了他，他的名字和文章才传遍了互联网。论“煽动”，抓他的人功劳最大。 独立中文笔会狱中作家委员会有一项工作：为因言获罪的作家、记者提供法律援助。原来的法律顾问是上海的郭国汀律师，他二〇〇五年出国后，由我接任。秘书长张裕让我联系李元龙的妻子杨秀敏。 杨秀敏已经在当地请了一位律师，不太满意，有朋友劝她辞掉。我劝她别辞：一个被告人可以请两个律师，有当地律师配合不是坏事；再说当事人单方解约，律师费也要不回来。她听了，寄来了委托书。 在此之前，我做过罗永忠案的二审，没有出庭；做杜导斌案，因为没经验跟警察起了冲突，中途夭折；张林案、师涛案，也只是见过当事人一面。李元龙案和差不多同时接手的杨天水案，是我第一次独立主办政治案件。好在张裕虽是理学博士，法律功底却很深，一直在网上帮我研究案情、拟辩护思路、改文书。 二 第一顿饭 二〇〇六年三月，我飞到贵阳。出机场已是深夜，杨秀敏和两个亲友在接机的人群里等我。我一张北方脸，他们一眼就认出来了。 我早听说贵州是中国民主党的重镇，民运人士很活跃。我担心他们介入会影响案子，再三叮嘱杨秀敏不要跟他们接触，我也不打算见他们。 她问我在贵阳有没有朋友。我说没有。其实我在政法大学读研时有个同学，正在贵州省科技厅当副厅长。可我办的是这种案子，他未必敢认我，说了也没意思。 从贵阳到毕节还有四百多里山路。第二天到了毕节，杨秀敏让我住她家，我为了上网，住进了一家有网线的宾馆——全毕节只有这一家，也是全毕节最贵的一家。 杨秀敏请的律师姓陈，西南政法毕业，做过十年法官，辞职当了律师，在当地很有名。杨秀敏说他水平高，脾气也大，她去得勤了，耽误他打牌，他几次说要解约。我劝她：有本事的人脾气大，有本事又受过挫折的，脾气更大。这种案子，当地律师肯接就不容易。 我们去找他时，他正在打牌，让我们在外间等。半小时后牌局散了，他出来拱拱手：李律师见谅，小地方，礼数不周。 陈律师四十岁上下，个子不高，脑子快，口才好。他先问我的学历——他从网上查到我在政法大学读过研究生。我说，我的律师资格是自学考出来的，比不了你们科班出身，读研就是去补课。他哈哈一笑，说话随便多了。 说到案子，他说： “这是本地的大案，办案的是国安，不是有人相托，我根本不接。你辩护完了拍拍屁股走人，我还要在这里吃饭。我当了十年法官，又做了这么多年律师，在这个环境里，把柄太多。我对李元龙这样的记者很佩服，可我自己放不开。你既然来了，咱们换个位置：你主辩，我配合。” 我答应了。他又说：要不要跟安全部门接触一下？你人生地不熟，交流交流，有利无害。 我听出了这句话的分量，飞快地算了算利害，说：可以，你安排。 他显然没想到我答应得这么痛快，反倒迟疑了：这样吧，你先回宾馆，晚上我请你吃饭。 晚上六点，陈律师开车来接我。我问跟安全部门见面的事，他支支吾吾：以后再说，今晚几个同学聚会，你一起去。别提李元龙的案子，也别说你从青岛来。 临走他让我带上电脑，说宾馆不安全。到了饭店门口，天下着小雨，他说：电脑放车里吧，你抱着喝酒，不怕丢？ 我心里明白了，把电脑交给了他。反正里面只有这个案子的资料和法律文书，没什么可保密的。 包厢里坐了十几个人，有男有女，派头都不小。陈律师介绍我是“北京来的张律师”；他们是局长、县长、队长、庭长，都是他的同学。只有一个年轻女子，看上去不像。 有人问我听不听得懂贵州话，我摇头傻笑。于是他们改说方言，放心大胆地聊。我走南闯北，贵州话能听懂三成，隐约听出他们在议论我的案子。 菜是辣的，酒是茅台，真正的茅台，一开瓶满屋子香。我喝了一杯就放下了。再劝，我就掏出一瓶药来——其实是我吃的胃药消食片——说正在吃药，真不能喝。这种案子，这帮人，这种酒，再喝两杯，我就别想站着出去。 席间那个年轻女子出去了一会儿。我借口洗手，出门看了看：陈律师的车不见了。 这顿饭吃到十点多。在座的都是吃工资的，我原以为要陈律师买单，那人情就大了。结果不是他买单。 散席后，陈律师和两个同学送我回宾馆。宾馆带洗浴中心，他们要去洗芬兰浴。我说房间里能洗，就不去了。陈律师不干：什么意思，不放心我？电脑在他车里，我只好跟着去。 洗了十分钟，我觉得不对，趁他们不注意，穿上衣服回了房间。 房间电话响个不停，都是“小姐”打来的。我把电话线拔了。 躺在床上，我想：如果我喝了酒，蒸了桑拿，进了KTV，再进来几个小姐，这会儿我该在公安分局了。 一点多，陈律师来电话：怎么一个人先走了？我说坐车累了。他说：电脑今晚还用吗？我还要喝个把小时茶。我说随便，今晚送回来就行。 三点多，他抱着电脑回来了，还醉着，打着酒嗝抱怨：你们北方人太狡猾，一个人溜了，让我自己对付那帮流氓。 他倒头就睡。我打开电脑，已经中了病毒，所有文件都打不开。 看着鼾声大作的陈律师，我心里说不清是轻蔑还是悲凉。当然，不全是冲着他。 三 “夜狼” 三月十四日上午，我和陈律师到毕节地区看守所会见李元龙。手续办得很顺，只是不许我把一本圣经带给他。 天冷，李元龙穿着一件军大衣，瘦，斯文，一副书生相，跟“夜狼”这个笔名毫不相干。 我问他起诉书收到没有，有什么想法。他说： “我承认自己‘有罪’，但我不承认他们的法律。那法律就是为我这样的人定的。我没想煽动颠覆国家政权，我只是想让这个国家走向民主、自由，和平转型。我错了吗？没有。” 文章是他写的，他认账。他不太会用电脑，文章都是先手写，再一个字一个字敲进去，权当练打字。邮件是上高中的儿子帮他发的，儿子不知道内容。 为什么写这些文章？他说，一是在党报整天说假话套话，憋得慌；二是贫富悬殊、官员腐败、司法不公，知识分子有义务说话；三是上网看到了外面的信息，思想变了。 我问他是怎么被盯上的。当时网上怀疑他像师涛一样，被美国网络公司出卖了。他说不是：第一篇文章《在思想上加入美国国籍》是儿子帮他发给《议报》的，四天后他上网一看，署的是真名“李元龙”。他赶紧托朋友打电话让编辑改成“夜狼”，可已经晚了。 他说，侦查期间压力极大，最受不了的是正读高三的儿子被牵连进来，传唤了三次。他精神几乎崩溃，为了儿子，说了不少自污的话。 那时我还没有信基督，对他这个基督徒这么轻易“认罪”很不理解，陈律师也很生气。后来我才懂：在基督徒看来，人人都是罪人，认罪不难。只是信仰里的罪和法律上的罪，根本是两回事。 会见快结束时，他拿出一封信。写信的是他资助的一个贫困女学生。她问：监狱不是关坏人的地方吗？您这样的好人，为什么也被关进去了？ 李元龙泪流满面。我和陈律师都答不上来。 四 爱如青山 毕节是古夜郎国故地，高原山区，土地贫瘠，交通闭塞。孩子失学，或者考上大学交不起学费，到处都是。 李元龙的朋友、毕节二中的徐老师交给我一份材料，记着李元龙这些年采写的助学报道和他自己资助学生的情况。七位老师、一些邻居和受助的学生在上面签了名。 一九九九年，孪生兄弟陈欢、陈乐分别考上北京化工大学和北方交大，母亲没有工作，丈夫早逝，拿不出学费。李元龙在《毕节日报》头版发了报道，各地捐款四万多元。兄弟俩又分出一部分，转助残疾同学。 二〇〇〇年，农村女孩徐晓英考上南昌航空工业学院，凑不出六七千元。李元龙写报道募到四千多元，又帮她办了五千元助学贷款，之后自己掏钱供她读完四年大学。 同一年，罗云武考上湖北经济学院，学杂费六千多，家里只有年迈的父亲种几分薄地。报到日期已过，他胸前挂着“求援助学”的纸牌，拿着录取通知书沿街乞讨。李元龙报道后，一家会计师事务所资助他读完大学。毕业后，他回到那家事务所工作。 二〇〇一年，周尚新以全省体育艺术类第一名考上北京体育大学，家里一贫如洗。李元龙的报道引来一位商人，一直资助他到毕业。 材料里列的，只是一部分。 一个地方小报的普通记者，凭一己之力，改变了几十个孩子的命运。他干的，本来是政府该干的事。 五 第二顿饭 下午我去法院递交手续。承办法官比我年轻，贵州大学法学院毕业，据说是业务骨干。他礼数周到，但不愿深谈，只收下了我的书面意见。后来我又寄过几份，他都一一呈报了上级。 第二天就要回青岛，我决定回请陈律师、徐老师和李元龙的朋友们。 徐老师和我年纪相仿，在网上读过我不少文章。我一到毕节，他就请我到家里吃了顿地道的贵州饭。他和笔会在当地的一位会员，都是那个“特殊部门”的“侦查对象”。我委婉地提醒他，他早就知道，毫不在意。我暗自惭愧——来贵州前，我还为要不要见当地的“敏感人士”犹豫了半天。 陈律师订的饭店，徐老师他们觉得不方便，我们冒雨另找了一家，再打电话叫陈律师。 陈律师带来一个年轻女子，说是助手。我们知道他离了婚，以为是女朋友，跟他开玩笑。一向能说会道的陈律师脸一红，一句话不说。那女子也一句话不说。 这一次，陈律师滴酒不沾。我倒放开了，喝了半斤多白酒，跟徐老师他们天南海北，敏感人物、敏感话题，一点不避讳。陈律师几次在桌下踩我的脚，我装不知道。中间那女子出去了五分钟，又回来了。 陈律师整晚只说了一句话：你不是不能喝酒吗？ 我说：病好了，可以喝了。 那天晚上，她录的音不会少于两盘磁带。 送我回宾馆时，那女子把一套卷宗复印件交给我。陈律师用力握了握我的手，说了三个字：多保重！ 六 庭外 回到青岛，我细读卷宗。陈律师几乎把整本预审卷都复印了，程序文书、证据材料，一应俱全，干净利落。到底是法官出身。 卷宗里看得出，检察院和安全厅意见并不一致。检察院起初不批捕，安全厅只好先监视居住。移送起诉后，检察院又对“捏造事实”的认定提出疑问：既然说李元龙文中关于中共执政以来非正常死亡数千万人、“六四”坦克杀人的说法是捏造，就该拿出真实的材料来。安全厅答复说，拿不出来。 这期间有两件事。一是国务院新闻办发言人对外国记者说，中国没有因言论被捕的作家、记者；二是胡锦涛将于四月访美。无国界记者和国际笔会都为李元龙案提出了抗议，访美期间可能会有记者提问。我把这些写进律师意见书，寄给法院和检察院。 法院取消了原定四月的开庭，但也没有放人。我寄希望于访美期间有记者当面提起此案。我不太相信胡锦涛会同意，因为四篇文章判一个记者坐牢。 结果，白宫南草坪的欢迎仪式上，一位法轮功背景的女记者突然高声抗议。此后胡锦涛在美期间不再举行记者会。李元龙的机会也没了。胡锦涛一回国，法院就定下五月十一日开庭。我知道，凶多吉少。 第一次去毕节让我明白，一个人闯毕节太危险。杨秀敏再提起贵州的陈西、廖双元等人想认识我、声援李元龙，我没再犹豫。 五月九日晚，陈西 [1] 和几位朋友在贵阳机场接我，连夜开车去毕节。 陈西原名陈友才，当过兵，入过党，做过金筑大学的政工干部。“六四”后，因组织“贵阳沙龙联谊会”等被判刑三年；一九九五年又因组建中国民主党贵州分部被判十年，二〇〇五年刚出狱。 他四十七八岁，平头，T恤短裤，目光温和，说话直率。我见过不少异议人士，大多辩才滔滔，你插不上嘴。陈西不一样，他多半在听，从不打断你。 我问他：贵州异议人士这么集中，活动也多，这几年却很少有人被抓，你们是怎么做到的？ 他说，第一是公开。理念公开——我们就是要搞多党政治，不讳言；活动公开——在宪法范围内活动，聚会前通知警方。时间长了，他们也习惯了。第二是不搞你死我活，非让步不可时也让一步。这次去毕节声援，警方不愿意，我们坚持，他们也只好默许。 我又问：贵州老百姓饭都吃不饱，关心民生多过民主。真实行了民主，民生怎么办？ 他说，先有民主，再厉行法治、铲除腐败，民生自然好办。 我有些失望，就借着夜路漫长，胡吹了一通：在贵州搞个民主特区，四周拉上铁丝网，开放党禁报禁，立法、行政、司法全部普选，媒体对全世界开放；投资移民解决资金，发展文化、新闻、旅游，把议会、法院变成景点，全国人民像当年参观大寨一样来参观。贵州在内陆，被各省围着，不怕搞独立，中央大可放心试验…… 陈西哈哈大笑：中共领导人要有这个胸襟，贵州幸甚，中华幸甚！可惜肉食者鄙，你我只能车上论政。 我知道这是闲扯。没想到一年后，陈西发表的贵州民主党人政治规划里，竟能看出这番话的影子。 那晚到了毕节，为了省钱，我们住进一家洗浴中心，洗了个热水澡，睡得很香。 北京的赵昕已经先到了。赵昕是八九学生领袖，也是维权人士、笔会会员、基督徒、民主党人。不久前他在四川旅行时被黑帮打断了腿，舆论认为背后有官方操纵。上一次李元龙案说要开庭，他就从云南老家悄悄赶来过。 如果说陈西是书生议政，赵昕就是活动家。第二天我去看守所和李元龙商量开庭的事，回来时，赵昕已经干成了一件“轰动世界”的事：他约了几位贵州朋友，到法院门口举着字拼成一副对联，拍照留念—— 夜郎还在自大，创钳制言论最恶案例；黔驴自然技穷，造侵犯人权极劣明证！ 照片很快上了海外媒体，路透社、法新社都追踪报道，毕节一下子成了新闻热点。 我心里不太痛快。这种街头抗议不会让法院心虚，只会让安全机关在《敌情通报》上多写一笔，正好把李元龙和“敌对势力”拴在一起。我也担心警方动手，为一个李元龙再搭进去几个人。 还好，他们没被驱逐，还进了法庭旁听。海外媒体说这是抗议的成果，我觉得是侥幸。后来陈光诚案开庭，同样的做法就没这么幸运：警方驱散人群，抓了十几个人。 七 法庭 五月十一日开庭。法院门口法警密布。旁听的人，包括律师，都要穿过一条弯弯曲曲的通道才能进法庭。我想起德国殖民时期在青岛建的法院，也有一条通往法庭的地下通道，专供犯人走。贺卫方教授说过，那是给犯人一个暗示：你是从地狱里出来的。毕节中院有没有这个用意，我不知道，但我确实尝到了被歧视的滋味。 四十八个旁听席，给李元龙的朋友留了四个，其余都是安全机关、党政机关和媒体的人。在前排安全厅的人中间，我看见了那天晚上陪陈律师吃饭的那个女子。散庭后，她直接坐安全厅的车走了，一点也不掩饰。 陈律师兑现约定，让我主辩。 公诉人金海雁，女，思路清楚，言辞锋利，准备得非常充分。我要引用的《约翰内斯堡原则》，她早已研究过，备好了反驳：那不是有约束力的国际条约，中国没有签署。我忍不住对她说：您是我见过的最优秀的公诉人。 指控的证据是四篇文章：《在思想上加入美国国籍》，赞美美国的民主自由，批评一党专制；《生的平凡，死的可悲》，重新评价刘胡兰和官方对她的宣传；《不光是八十老母去世还要继续开会的书记》，批评一个老母去世仍坚持开会的书记；《从百岁老朽入党说开去》，讽刺基层党组织吸收百岁老人入党作秀。 我的意见是：这些都是作者的价值判断，有的言辞过激，但批评的都是具体的人、事和历史，属于宪法第三十五条保护的言论自由，没有一个字涉及颠覆国家政权、推翻社会主义制度。 公诉人的重点是“捏造事实”：中共伙同国民党屠杀三千万人，“六四”坦克杀人。我说，前后十几年内战的死亡人数远不止三千万，再加上“三年自然灾害”和“文革”的非正常死亡，总数在八千万上下，这不是李元龙杜撰的。至于“六四”坦克杀人，安全机关自己承认拿不出否定的证据，凭什么说是捏造？ 下午辩论。公诉人的意见归结起来是三条：没有共产党就没有社会主义中国，攻击党就是要颠覆政权；文章语言恶毒，已超出言论自由；被告人多次认罪，有供述为证。 我说，公诉人的逻辑是“党即国家”：批评党等于攻击党，攻击党等于颠覆党的执政地位，颠覆执政地位等于颠覆国家政权。这中间每一道鸿沟是怎么跨过去的，我看不出来。 公诉人说，文章发表后“被多人次点击并回复”，危害了国家政权。我说，一共二十五人次回复，还有人表示反对。人民民主专政的政权，难道是风一吹就倒的林妹妹？ 公诉人说，李元龙“明知”文章可能导致他人颠覆国家政权。我说，这真是抬举他了，几篇文章成了精神原子弹。网上比这激烈得多的文字每天浩如烟海，真有这么大威力，政权早就灰飞烟灭了，怎么还坚如磐石，还有能力把李元龙关进大牢？ 我和公诉人正辩得热闹，整个上午一言不发的陈律师突然开口了。 他说：公诉人反复宣读的“认罪供述”不能作为证据。国安在侦查期间把李元龙的儿子羁押了一个星期，把杨秀敏软禁在旅馆十来天，又威胁李元龙：不老实认罪，儿子要受牵连。那是一个十六岁、品学兼优、正面临高考的孩子。李元龙是在这种情况下写下《我的反党反社会主义自白书》的。这份自白书证明不了被告人有罪，只能证明办案人员违法。请审判长查明，不予采纳。 旁听席上的陈西、赵昕，连整个法庭，都吃了一惊。旁听席上响起了掌声。陈西事后说，陈律师敢直指强力机关违法，实在出乎意料。 最后陈述，李元龙说： “我是否触犯法律，我不清楚，我不是法律人。我批评共产党，揭露个别党员的丑行，有这回事，用的是文学语言，有些过火。但那是宪法给公民的批评权和言论自由。 我不是破坏者，不是敌人。我是一个热爱这片土地的基督徒。我爱每一个爱我和恨我的人，包括把我当敌人的人。 这块土地不再需要敌人。我还有许多事要做，一些贫困学生、一些孤儿需要我的帮助，我对他们有过承诺。 审判长，我相信邪不压正！” 他说完，法庭里好一会儿没有声音。 下午四点半休庭，没有当庭宣判。 这就是当年的江湖：酒里有局，包里有毒，身边有鬼，但庭上……还有戏。 八 尾声 七月十二日，一审判决：有期徒刑二年，剥夺政治权利二年。李元龙上诉，二审维持原判。 很多在网上写文章批评执政党的人问：四篇文章判两年，我该判几年？ 刑期不满三年，李元龙留在看守所服刑。贵州太远，我再没去看过他，只和杨秀敏通信。我寄给她一本我在香港出的书，里面有我写李元龙的文章。她回信道谢，附了一篇写丈夫的文章。 杨秀敏比李元龙小很多。李元龙离婚后，她不顾家里和旁人的反对嫁给他，和他一起抚养前妻留下的儿子。人人都知道李元龙有才华，很少有人知道杨秀敏也是才女。那篇文章写丈夫的为人，写因言获罪给一个家留下的伤，文笔凄美，读来令人神伤。 二〇〇七年春节前，杨秀敏打来电话，声音里透着高兴：狱方说，只要李元龙“认罪伏法”，可以减刑，春节前放他回家过年。 我也高兴，又不敢太乐观。我们商量了半天，最后她说：我就怕他不肯，他那个宁折不弯的脾气。 这也是我担心的。他是个温和的人，可说起自己做的事对不对，神色坚定，口气决绝。 果然，后来就没了消息。春节过后，杨秀敏也没再来电话。我不忍心问。我知道，他要坐满“法律”给他的两年，来证明他对信念的忠诚。 那个给他写信的女学生，在他出狱后到了青岛。我安排她读书，帮她找了一份工作。 我书房的窗外是一座青山。春天山花烂漫，夏天青峰挺立，秋天果香弥漫，冬天雪压云低。为他辩护的时候，我一直想不通：一个温和、满怀爱心的基督徒，怎么会用那样尖刻的语言批评掌权的人？有一天看着那座山，我忽然懂了：造物主的造物，有烂漫，也有咆哮；有奉献，也有孤傲。四季合在一起，才是她的大爱。 李元龙的爱，就是那座青山。 （2007年5月初稿于青岛虎山居，2026年改定） [1] 陈西，贵州著名民主党人、异议作家，二〇一一年十二月再次以煽动颠覆国家政权罪被判刑十年。

title: Observations from Taiwan’s Education Frontline amid Cognitive Warfare
zh_title: 认知战中台湾教育前线的观察
summary: 下载整期 PDF 作为全球台湾研究所致力于促进声音多元化的一部分，全球台湾简报偶尔会发表台湾年轻人撰写的文章。我们很高兴以一名高中生的视角来阐述年轻人在复杂的互联网信息环境中所面临的挑战，以及台湾学校关于公民教育的持续争论。台湾面临着一些严重的威胁，不仅来自直接的军事力量，还来自我在同龄人中经常看到的自我挫败的态度。虽然在国外
content:
下载整期 PDF 作为全球台湾研究所致力于促进声音多元化的一部分，全球台湾简报偶尔会发表台湾年轻人撰写的文章。我们很高兴以一名高中生的视角来阐述年轻人在复杂的互联网信息环境中所面临的挑战，以及台湾学校关于公民教育的持续争论。台湾面临着一些严重的威胁，不仅来自直接的军事力量，还来自我在同龄人中经常看到的自我挫败的态度。尽管外国观察家警告两岸可能发生冲突，但年轻人流行的社交媒体平台上却充斥着“战争不会爆发”、“台湾无论如何也不会赢”或“谁统治我们并不重要”等言论。但这些言论并不代表台湾大多数青年群体的声音，也不应被视为整个一代人放弃的证据。然而，随着对民主的冷漠成为日常谈话的一部分，它产生了一种值得关注的脆弱性。问题的出现并不仅仅是因为一些学生对政治了解太少。事实上，我们许多人在与我们学校设计的环境截然不同的信息环境中遭遇政治。公民教育仍然主要通过教科书、考试和课堂讲座进行。
然而，政治叙事现在通过短视频、影响者、模因和推荐算法传达给我们。如果学校以中立的名义避免讨论有争议的问题，学生将不会变得政治中立：相反，他们会去其他地方学习政治。当政治通过信息传播时 中国社交媒体平台已成为台湾信息环境的重要组成部分。 TikTok、抖音和 Rednote 等平台模糊了娱乐和政治影响力之间的界限。事实上，可能影响台湾人的内容并不总是需要采用明显的宣传。现代天际线、高铁、传统文化、美食、乡村生活、普通家庭的视频都能让中国成为一个熟悉而有吸引力的国家。政治信息可以通过娱乐视频传播，而台湾年轻人可能根本不认为这些是政治信息。这不是一个边缘问题。事实上，Doublethink Lab 2025 年的一项研究（使用台湾传播调查的数据）发现，50.73% 的高中生使用 TikTok。研究人员还采访了 16 名 15 岁至 18 岁的台湾用户，发现政治视频有时会意外地出现在社交媒体群组中，尤其是在 2024 年总统选举前后。尽管如此，研究人员发现，大多数青少年仍然对中华人民共和国政府持负面看法，反对统一。
因此，声称使用中国平台会让台湾青少年“亲中国”的说法过于简单化。更重要的问题可能是台湾年轻人在这些平台上遇到什么样的政治信息，以及他们如何理解这些信息。当我们超越屏幕上出现的内容时，这种担忧变得更加清晰。 2025 年对 700 名台湾 Z 世代成员进行的一项同行评审研究发现，更频繁地使用中国社交媒体平台（包括 TikTok、Rednote 和微博）与对两岸事务的政治了解较低有关

【原文 English Original】
DOWNLOAD FULL ISSUE PDF As part of the Global Taiwan Institute’s commitment to promoting a diversity of voices, the Global Taiwan Brief occasionally publishes articles written by Taiwanese youth. We are pleased to present this perspective from a high school student about the challenges young people face in navigating a complex internet information environment, and continuing debates over civic education in Taiwan’s schools. Taiwan faces several serious threats, not only from direct military forces, but also from a self-defeating attitude that I see frequently in people of my age. While foreign observers warn of the possibility of a cross-Strait conflict, social media platforms popular among young people are filled with claims that “War won’t break out,” “Taiwan could never win anyway,” or “It doesn’t matter who governs us.” Nonetheless, these statements do not represent the voice of the majority of youth groups in Taiwan, and they should not be seen as proof that the entire generation has given up. However, as indifference toward democracy becomes a part of everyday conversation, it creates a sort of vulnerability that deserves attention. The problem arises not simply because some students know too little about politics. In fact, many of us encounter politics in an information environment very different from the one for which our schools were designed. Civic education still largely proceeds through textbooks, exams, and classroom lectures. Political narratives, however, now reach us through short videos, influencers, memes, and recommendation algorithms. If schools avoid discussing controversial issues in the name of neutrality, students will not become politically neutral: instead, they will go somewhere else to learn about politics. When Politics Spreads Through the Feed Chinese social media platforms have become a major part of Taiwan’s information environment. Platforms such as TikTok, Douyin, and Rednote blur the line between entertainment and political influence. Indeed, content that may impact Taiwanese does not always have to employ obvious propaganda. Videos of modern skylines , high-speed rail, traditional culture, food, rural life, or ordinary families can render China a familiar and attractive country. Political messages can then spread through entertainment videos, and Taiwanese youth may not perceive these as political messages at all. This is not a marginal issue. In fact, a 2025 Doublethink Lab study —using data from the Taiwan Communication Survey—found that 50.73 percent of high-school students used TikTok. Researchers also interviewed sixteen Taiwanese users aged fifteen to eighteen and discovered that political videos had sometimes appeared unexpectedly in social media groups, especially around the 2024 presidential election. Nonetheless, the researchers found that most of these teenagers still had negative views of the PRC government and opposed unification. It is thus an oversimplification to claim that using Chinese platforms makes Taiwanese teenagers “pro-China.” The more important question may be what kind of political information Taiwanese youth encounter on those platforms, and how they understand it. That concern becomes clearer when we look beyond what appears on the screen. A 2025 peer-reviewed study of 700 members of Taiwan’s Generation Z found that more frequent use of Chinese social media platforms—including TikTok, Rednote, and Weibo—was associated with lower political knowledge about cross-Strait affairs, and a weaker ability to tell the different usages of language between China and Taiwan. Greater use of Chinese social media was also linked to a decreased ability to identify People’s Republic of China (PRC) disinformation. This does not necessarily mean that young people are being “brainwashed.” The problem may be more subtle. If people have less knowledge about an issue, it becomes harder for them to judge whether the information they see is reliable in the first place. The numbers from another Doublethink Lab nationwide survey make this picture even more complicated. Among 2,612 Taiwanese respondents aged fifteen and above, the majority of both frequent and non-frequent TikTok users rejected the idea of giving up democracy for cross-Strait peace. Yet there was still a difference between the frequent and non-frequent users. The study found that 30.3 percent of frequent users were willing to accept giving up democracy for peace, compared with 23.4 percent of non-frequent users. Frequent users were also more likely to believe that unification with China might not significantly change everyday life in Taiwan. These numbers do not prove that TikTok caused these attitudes. But they do suggest that cognitive influence does not have to make young Taiwanese actively admire Beijing. Sometimes, it may simply make the differences between democratic and authoritarian systems feel less important, or make resistance seem less worthwhile. What “Politics Out of Schools” Originally Meant If political influence increasingly reaches students through their phones, then Taiwan must also ask what role schools should play. Here, our democratic history creates an ironic situation. During the authoritarian period of Taiwan, politics was not absent from Taiwanese campuses. Rather, politics was deeply intertwined with education. Historical records show that Kuomintang (國民黨) organizations, the China Youth Corps (中國青年救國團), military instructors, and state security agencies were involved in monitoring and managing university campuses. In 1986 and 1987, as Taiwan moved toward democratization, students involved in the “Freedom of Love” movement (自由之愛運動) at National Taiwan University demanded freedom of speech, university autonomy, and reform of the University Act (大學法) , as well as the removal of party organizations, the Youth Corps, and military instructors from campuses. This history matters because the original democratic demand was not that students should stop discussing politics. Instead, it was that the party-state should stop controlling political life in schools. Indeed, demands for political institutions to leave campuses appeared alongside demands for greater freedom of expression. Removing political control is not the same as removing political discussion. Taiwan’s legal framework still reflects this distinction. Article 6 of the Educational Fundamental Act (教育基本法) requires education to follow a principle of neutrality and prohibits schools from either campaigning for particular political organizations, or forcing teachers and students to participate in political activities. The restriction is directed at the institution, not at the student. Taiwan democratized its schools by making institutions politically neutral, not by requiring students to be politically silent. Image: A teacher and students at Baozhong Junior High School in Yunlin County, Taiwan (December 2019). Image source: Wikimedia Commons ) From Political Neutrality to Political Silence Yet in practice, the memory of authoritarian political indoctrination may have encouraged a broader habit of avoiding controversial politics in school. The idea that “politics should not enter schools” (政治不入校園) can be interpreted not only as a warning against party control, but also as a reason for teachers to avoid politically sensitive issues. This is different from the original purpose of educational neutrality, which was to protect students from forced ideology, rather than to stop them from discussing political life. The same tension can also be seen inside schools. A National Academy for Educational Research (國家教育研究院) survey of high-school history teachers found broad support for teaching transitional justice, but more than 60 percent of teachers worried that such teaching could be influenced by partisan viewpoints. Among teachers who did not design additional lessons on transitional justice, fear of being accused of partisan indoctrination was the second most common reason— after lack of class time. This does not mean that teachers do not want to discuss politics. Rather, it shows how easily civic education can be confused with political indoctrination, even in a democratic society. The tension is especially clear because Taiwan’s curriculum has moved in the opposite direction. The 108 Curriculum (108課綱) included transitional justice in high-school history, and education researchers have also recommended using multiple historical perspectives to encourage discussion and reflection. Formally, schools are therefore expected to help students think critically about history, understand different perspectives, and reflect on democratic values. At the same time, teachers may still worry about being accused of taking sides. As many of my classmates have noticed, political issues can therefore become exam facts that we memorize for answer sheets, but quickly escape our memory. Civics exists as an academic subject, but politics does not always become part of students’ real lives. History can feel distant from our own identities, while democratic rights become background conditions that we assume will always exist. When students then hear “If there’s war, just surrender” or “It doesn’t matter who is in charge,” they may understand the danger of war without having seriously thought about what political change could mean for freedom of speech, elections, personal rights, or the rule of law. This is where the role of the classroom becomes important. Schools should not tell students which party to support or what position to take on cross-Strait relations. Instead, they should give students a place to ask questions, test claims, compare evidence, and discuss difficult issues. Research using data from 3,953 Taiwanese students in the International Civic and Citizenship Education Study found that an open classroom climate for discussion was associated with stronger civic knowledge and expected electoral participation. In other words, students do not become better citizens simply because disagreement is kept out of the classroom. They need opportunities to learn how to disagree while still respecting evidence, rights, and one another. Rebuilding Civic Resilience Taiwan can learn from the experiences of other democracies. Austria has included political education in its formal education system and emphasizes that controversial issues should also be presented as controversial in the classroom, while avoiding political indoctrination. Finland , meanwhile, treats media literacy as an important part of education and integrates it across subjects, helping students understand information, media, and misleading content. These two examples show that political education and media literacy do not have to mean telling students what to believe. Instead, they can help students understand political issues, recognize different viewpoints, and evaluate the information they receive. Taiwan has also begun to recognize this need. In 2025, the Ministry of Education (教育部) announced plans to develop teaching materials on understanding China, including cross-Strait relations, national identity, and possible risks. By July 2025 , thirteen teaching materials had undergone initial review, and were still being revised and supplemented. However, as a student on the front line of Taiwan’s education system, I was barely aware of this plan. Most of the teachers and classmates I asked had not heard about it either. Even if the material is still under review, students should be able to understand what is being prepared, why it is needed, and when they may actually have the chance to use it. A policy cannot have much effect on students if the students themselves barely possess awareness of it. For this reason, the Taiwanese government should expedite the development of these materials and simultaneously seek to raise awareness among students and teachers regarding what changes are underway. However, teaching materials alone may not be enough. Taiwan should also consider adding more opportunities for civic education and discussion in schools, especially on topics such as cross-Strait relations, democracy, media literacy, and how political information affects our daily lives. Taiwan does not need to copy either Austria or Finland’s models exactly. Its own history provides the more important lesson. Taiwan’s democratization movement fought to remove one-party control from schools so that thought could become freer. The purpose of that effort was never to create classrooms in which politics could not be discussed. Modern cognitive warfare makes this distinction urgent. Algorithms do not respect the principle of “politics out of schools.” They enter teenagers’ lives every day, deciding what we see. If schools in democracies respond by remaining silent, they leave the most politically consequential part of students’ education to systems designed not to educate citizens, but to maximize attention. The challenge, then, is not to bring partisan politics back into schools. It is to bring democratic politics back into civic education. Students should understand how Taiwan’s freedoms were won, how authoritarian systems differ from democratic ones, how algorithms can shape political perception, and how to examine claims without automatically accepting or rejecting them because of party labels. Taiwan’s psychological defense will not be built by teaching young people what to think. It will be built by giving them the knowledge and habits necessary to decide what is worth defending for themselves. The main point: As political information increasingly reaches Taiwanese youth through social media, schools’ reluctance to discuss controversial issues may leave students more vulnerable to misleading narratives and cognitive influence. Political neutrality should not mean political silence. Instead, Taiwan’s civic education should encourage open discussion, critical thinking, and media literacy, allowing students to develop their own informed judgments about democracy and the challenges it faces. The Death of Logic and Sanity in Silicon Valley bbert@hudson.org Tue, 11/24/2026 - 13:49 SVG Commentary Nov 24, 2026 Washington Times The Death of Logic and Sanity in Silicon Valley Our technology giants are helping China challenge American supremacy   Miles Yu Senior Fellow and Director, China Center Miles Yu Commentary Caption The headquarters of NVIDIA in the Silicon Valley, Santa Clara, California, November 6, 2025. (Getty Images) Toggle Table of Contents Contents Contents Share to Twitter Twitter Share to Facebook Facebook Share to LinkedIn LinkedIn Share to E-mail E-mail Print Print Something has gone terribly wrong in Silicon Valley . The industry that made America the world’s technological superpower has produced executives whose commercial ambitions increasingly collide with national security. Their dealings with communist China expose an astonishing paradox: American technology companies help China catch up with the United States, then warn that China is catching up, and finally use that warning to demand permission to sell China even more advanced technology. No one is more vocal in advancing this lunacy than Nvidia’s now-reinstated CEO Jensen Huang . Mr. Huang’s latest scandal has been sensationalized, focusing on his illicit relationship with Alice Huang, a Chinese national and a former executive of Singapore-based Megaspeed . Yet the bigger issue is Mr. Huang’s absurd ideas about China and its artificial intelligence industry. Mr. Huang has repeatedly argued that China is catching up with or even winning the AI race, that American export controls are futile or “the dumbest thing we’ve ever done” and that restricting advanced chip sales to China will ultimately undermine American technological leadership. He says those resisting his ideas — whom he labels “ China hawks” — are unpatriotic and un-American. These arguments are intellectually vacuous, characteristically arrogant, strategically reckless and remarkably self-seeking for Nvidia’s commercial interests. Worse, they reflect a broader Silicon Valley mentality that confuses corporate profits with America’s national interest. Consider the contradictions. If China is winning the AI race, why are Chinese companies so desperate for Nvidia’s advanced chips? If American AI models such as Claude and ChatGPT are losing their technological edge, why do China’s top AI firms, such as Kimi and Alibaba, seek to extract their capabilities through large-scale distillation? If American export controls are futile, why does Beijing devote extraordinary resources to circumventing them? How can supplying America’s foremost strategic adversary with the technologies underpinning American supremacy possibly strengthen America’s competitive advantage? Mr. Huang’s vicious dismissal of “ China hawks” as wearing a “badge of shame” makes defending American technological superiority sound disgraceful whenever it interferes with corporate profits. His arguments collapse under the absurdity of their own logic. In fact, this is Silicon Valley’s self-fulfilling prophecy, a circular argument that converts the consequences of its own commercial decisions into justification for repeating them. China’s technological progress remains critically dependent on American semiconductor designs, advanced AI chips, computing infrastructure and technical expertise. Without access to these capabilities, Beijing would face far greater obstacles in developing cutting-edge AI. China’s scientists and engineers are capable, and its government invests enormous resources in innovation. Yet its relentless pursuit of American technology reveals how much its technological ambitions still depend on foreign breakthroughs. Mr. Huang’s corporate behavior is also in question. Multiple reports indicate that Megaspeed has purchased more than $4.8 billion in advanced Nvidia AI chips since June 2024 and has erased the records of these transactions from its books. American authorities have investigated suspected diversion through Southeast Asian intermediaries. Reports have also raised questions about Ms. Huang’s suspected ties to Chinese intelligence. Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter reportedly contacted Commerce Department investigators, citing clearance from Undersecretary Jeffrey Kessler, regarding the Megaspeed investigation. Nvidia denies wrongdoing and says it stopped supplying Megaspeed in June 2025, but recent reports dispute the denial. Congress and law enforcement should investigate the Megaspeed affair, examine possible interference with export-control enforcement and close loopholes involving third-country intermediaries, remote computing access and sensitive technology licensing. Proven violations deserve serious penalties. Nvidia is hardly alone. Consider Advanced Micro Devices CEO Lisa Su, Mr. Huang’s distant cousin. In 2016, under her leadership, AMD entered into a technology-licensing agreement worth approximately $293 million, plus royalties, with Chinese partners affiliated with the Chinese Academy of Sciences. The arrangement transferred valuable x86-compatible processor technology and first-generation Zen intellectual property into China’s industrial ecosystem. The available record indicates the transaction was lawful. Its strategic wisdom deserves scrutiny. Why should American companies help develop China’s indigenous computing capabilities and then warn Americans about the technological challenge they helped create? Cisco provides another cautionary example. Falun Gong practitioners accused the company of supplying technologies that helped China’s Golden Shield surveillance system identify and track religious believers. Cisco disputed the allegations, and this year the U.S. Supreme Court dismissed the lawsuit, holding that the Alien Tort Statute does not allow aiding-and-abetting liability against corporations. Yet the controversy illustrates the risks of American technology becoming entangled with authoritarian surveillance. The Chinese Communist Party systematically mobilizes civilian technology for military modernization, intelligence operations and political control. U.S. executives advocating greater access to technology for China must confront these strategic consequences. America’s technological supremacy rests on decades of innovation, enormous investment and hard-won expertise. Allowing these advantages to strengthen its principal strategic adversary threatens the foundations of American security. Silicon Valley has perfected a vicious cycle of strategic folly: Sell advanced American technology to China , often knowingly and furtively through a third, surrogate country such as Singapore. Watch Beijing close the gap. Warn Americans that China is catching up. Declare export controls futile. Demand permission to sell even more advanced technology to China . Repeat. Each turn enriches Silicon Valley , strengthens Beijing and erodes America’s technological supremacy. The closer China gets, the louder the alarm — and the louder the alarm, the greater the pressure to sell China more. Eventually, the prophecy fulfills itself: Silicon Valley helps China catch up, warns America that China is catching up, and uses that warning to help China catch up even faster, until America loses the race its own technology giants helped China win. In other words, Silicon Valley has lost its mind. In explaining his support for Mr. Huang’s reinstatement, President Trump has said Mr. Huang has learned his lessons. Let us hope these lessons learned will help Silicon Valley regain its sanity. Read in the Washington Times. Enjoyed this analysis? 封面图片：图片联盟/共同社 11 月 19 日，美国总统唐纳德·特朗普在深圳与中国领导人习近平和俄罗斯总统弗拉基米尔·普京会面后承认，“一旦拥有核武器，就很难不拥有核武器”。这一困难体现在他们的“共同和平宣言”中关于这一主题的谦虚和不置可否的语言，三位领导人重申了里根-戈尔巴乔夫的声明，即“核战争不可能获胜，也决不能打”，并同意“就减少核风险和防止核武器扩散进行对话”。这并不完全是特朗普在峰会前推动的“无核化”谈判。尽管如此，世界三大核大国罕见的共同语言可能有助于为更实质性的接触奠定一些政治基础。随着中国扩大其核武库以及所有三个国家都进行核现代化，就避免误解和误判的措施达成三边协议将符合每个人的利益。存在与声明中的语言相匹配的合理步骤。然而，正如特朗普所发现的那样，中国需要大量说服才能放弃其对与美国签署核协议的传统反对态度。欧洲两个拥核国家英国和法国也不愿参与，但这样做可能有助于让中国加入。从小事做起 这一切来得太早了。
《新削减战略武器条约》（New START）对美国和俄罗斯的战略核力量设定了具有约束力的限制，该条约于 2026 年 2 月到期，尽管两国继续实施冷战期间谈判达成的一系列核风险削减措施。北京与莫斯科签署的此类协议少得多，与华盛顿签署的此类协议也几乎没有。除了其内在价值外，旨在减少核风险的新三边协议将有助于履行三个国家在《核不扩散条约》下的义务，即“承诺就停止核军备竞赛的有效措施进行谈判……”。更可行的短期选择之一是三边导弹发射前通知（PLN）协议，该协议通过在使用某些导弹和太空运载火箭（SLV）之前告知对方，帮助各国避免误解和误判。美国和俄罗斯有这样的协议，中国和俄罗斯也有这样的协议。尽管北京方面驳斥了承诺遵守任何新的PLN协议的呼吁，但它还是主动向美国和其他国家通报了其于2024年和2026年两次向太平洋进行潜射弹道导弹的试验，这表明它看到了这项措施的价值。
为了确保潜在的PLN快速、安全地到达，并提供危机沟通渠道，中国还可以同意建立一个相当于美国和俄罗斯已有的核风险降低中心的国家级中心。这些中心昼夜不停地运作，例如在2001年9月11日被用来向克里姆林宫领导人保证美国的防御姿态并非针对俄罗斯。未来，三方可能会更加雄心勃勃地同意限制可供使用的洲际导弹和轰炸机的数量。正如军控学者杰弗里·刘易斯 (Jeffrey Lewis) 指出的那样，中国不太可能突破已过期的《削减战略武器条约》中规定的 700 辆部署车辆的限制，即使要装载

【原文 English Original】
Cover image: picture alliance / Kyodo “Once you have the nuclear weapons, it’s very hard to not have them,” conceded US president Donald Trump after his meeting in Shenzhen with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian president Vladimir Putin on November 19th. This difficulty was reflected in the modest and non-committal language on the topic in their “ joint declaration towards peace ”, with the three leaders reaffirming the Reagan-Gorbachev statement that “a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought” and agreeing to “conduct a dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons”. This was not quite the “denuclearisation” talks that Trump had pushed for in the run-up to the summit. Nevertheless, the rare joint language from the world’s three biggest nuclear powers could help lay some political foundations for more substantial engagement. As China expands its arsenal and all three countries undertake nuclear modernisation, trilateral agreements on measures to avoid misperception and miscalculation would be in everyone’s interest. Plausible steps exist to match the language in the declaration. Yet, as Trump has found, it will take a lot of persuasion for China to drop its traditional opposition to nuclear agreements with America. Europe’s two nuclear-armed states, Britain and France, will also be reluctant to participate—but doing so may help get China on board. Starting small This would not come a moment too soon. The New Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty (New START), which set binding limits on American and Russian strategic nuclear forces, expired in February 2026, though the two countries continue to implement a range of nuclear-risk reduction measures they negotiated during the cold war. Beijing has far fewer such agreements with Moscow and barely any with Washington. Besides their intrinsic value, new trilateral agreements to reduce nuclear risk would constitute progress towards fulfilling the three countries’ obligation under the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty to “undertake to pursue negotiations… on effective measures relating to cessation of the nuclear arms race”. Among the more feasible short-term options is a trilateral missile pre-launch notification (PLN) agreement, which helps states avoid misperception and miscalculation by telling each other ahead of their use of certain missiles and space-launch vehicles (SLV). America and Russia have such an agreement, so do China and Russia. Even though Beijing has rebuked calls to commit to any new PLN agreements, it voluntarily pre-notified America and other countries of its two tests of submarine-launched ballistic missiles into the Pacific Ocean in 2024 and 2026, suggesting it sees value in the measure.   To ensure potential PLNs arrive quickly and securely, and to provide a channel for crisis communications, China could also agree to establish a national equivalent of the nuclear risk reduction centres that already exist in the US and Russia. These centres operate around the clock, and were used, for example, on September 11th 2001 to reassure leaders in the Kremlin that America’s defensive posture was not aimed at Russia. In the future, and far more ambitiously, the three parties could agree to limit the numbers of intercontinental missiles and bombers that are ready for use. As arms-control scholar Jeffrey Lewis notes , China is unlikely to cross the limit of 700 deployed vehicles specified in the expired START, even if it were to load all of its launchers with missiles. As such, a voluntary trilateral commitment to observing this limit could be palatable to the country. Without a formal verification system, however, such an agreement could become unstable. The missing side of the triangle Measures like these could help Trump move closer to fulfilling his longstanding arms-control ambitions. During his first term, he tried unsuccessfully to bring China into trilateral arms-control talks. More recently, citing China’s nuclear build-up, second Trump administration officials once again called for multilateral talks with a view to negotiating a successor to New START. The second administration’s engagement with China on nuclear-risk reduction constitutes a continuation of the Biden agenda . US and Chinese delegations met in November 2023 for what China termed “consultations” on arms control and non-proliferation, where the US side pushed for greater Chinese nuclear transparency and efforts to reduce strategic risks. These talks reportedly yielded little progress and China later suspended them citing US arms sales to Taiwan. Chinese officials have repeatedly pointed to the smaller size of China’s nuclear arsenal relative to those of America and Russia, and the resulting “special and primary responsibilities” of the other two powers to reduce their arsenals first But Beijing has also long maintained a more fundamental aversion to nuclear arms control with Washington. Chinese officials have repeatedly pointed to the smaller size of China’s nuclear arsenal relative to those of America and Russia, and the resulting “special and primary responsibilities” of the other two powers to reduce their arsenals first. China’s 2025 white paper on arms control acknowledges its interest in nuclear risk reduction but its answer to the challenge has been a proposal for adoption of China’s policy of nuclear no-first-use across the five permanent members of the UN Security Council, which has been criticised as unenforceable and potentially counterproductive. Where Europe comes in The nuclear point in the Shenzhen declaration does not call for the inclusion of Britain and France (the other two permanent Security Council members) in risk-reduction dialogue. But Russian officials have previously pushed for their inclusion in any multilateral arms-control talks. Like China, however, the two European powers have been historically reluctant to agree to any such talks outside the existing process among the five permanent members, mainly because of their comparatively smaller nuclear arsenals. In the coming years, even accounting for the announced increases in both the British and the French arsenals, China’s projected nuclear force will far surpass both. In addition, a (seemingly well-founded ) fear for Europeans will be whether any US engagement on arms control with Russia comes at the cost of concessions on Ukraine. Still, Britain and France joining the measures outlined above would be relatively low-cost and a net positive, and could perhaps help bring China on board. Britain and France already pre-notify their missile and SLV launches voluntarily through the Hague Code of Conduct against Ballistic Missile Proliferation mechanism . Establishing risk reduction centres in Europe would bring a new secure crisis-communications channel, which would be especially useful given tensions with Russia. A limit on missiles and launchers would not meaningfully constrain the two European countries because of differences in their force structures. But it would still likely prove politically acceptable to them, at least in the short term.   *** With no more formal limits on US and Russian strategic arsenals, the imperative to pursue nuclear risk-reduction measures is only intensifying. But it will indeed be “very hard” to turn political declarations into agreements, and any future dialogue may well get stuck on the countries’ varying perceptions of nuclear responsibilities and the origins of nuclear risk. Still, the Trump administration is highly motivated to pursue arms control, and—despite the symbolism and subtext of the Shenzhen meeting—this aspect of the resulting declaration may ultimately benefit Europeans, who also have an interest in persuading China to join trilateral measures. Chinese v American Views on WAR with Taiwan
Posted Aug 14, 2026 by Martin Armstrong |
The Center for Strategic and International Studies conducted an extraordinary survey of 64 leading experts on China, Taiwan, and cross-Strait relations, including 28 former senior U.S. government officials, 23 former government policy and intelligence analysts, and 13 academics and think-tank experts. What their answers reveal is not that China is preparing to invade Taiwan tomorrow, as the neocons would like everyone to believe, but that Beijing remains willing to wait so long as nobody crosses the line of formal Taiwanese independence. Some 84% said Beijing is willing to wait for unification but will not accept the status quo permanently, while only 10% believed China seeks unification at the earliest opportunity. Not one of the 64 experts believed Beijing would ever accept an independent Taiwan.
This is precisely why Taiwan has become so dangerous. The West keeps portraying the conflict as if Xi Jinping wakes up every morning staring at a calendar trying to decide when to launch an amphibious invasion. Yet 83% of these experts said China did not plan to use significant kinetic force against Taiwan by 2027, and 80% said China’s enormous 2022 military exercises did not indicate Beijing had accelerated its timetable. Only 6% of respondents outside the former senior government group saw 2027 as a hard deadline, while not one former senior U.S. official did. The obsession with 2027 has nevertheless become extremely useful for the military establishment because every supposed deadline becomes another justification for weapons, deployments, bases, and spending.
The survey found that 44% believed Beijing has a hard deadline of 2049, the centennial of the People’s Republic, while 42% believed China could wait indefinitely provided unification remains possible. This is an important distinction because China thinks in terms of generations while Western politicians think in terms of the next election. Beijing does not need to invade Taiwan if economic, political, and military pressure can gradually change the situation in its favor. Only 20% of those surveyed believed China even possessed a coherent roadmap for peaceful unification, which tells us this is not some perfectly scripted invasion plan sitting in Xi’s desk drawer.
Where the numbers become alarming is not an unprovoked invasion but what happens when politicians begin crossing China’s red lines. More than three-quarters of the experts, 77%, believed China would invade within six months if Taiwan formally declared independence. Among former senior U.S. officials, that number was 79%. Even some of those who did not expect an immediate invasion believed Beijing would respond with a blockade or enormous military exercises. This is why politicians encouraging Taiwan toward formal independence are playing with the lives of 23 million people. They can deliver all the speeches they want about democracy from Washington, London, or Brussels, but they will not be the civilians sitting underneath the missiles if their political experiment goes wrong.
Not one expert believed an explicit American commitment to defend Taiwan would cause China to invade immediately, but 64% believed Beijing would respond strongly enough to provoke a U.S.-China or China-Taiwan crisis, while another 31% expected a more limited negative response. Only two of the 64 experts believed formally committing America to Taiwan’s defense would actually deter China from using force because Beijing already assumes that the United States will intervene anyway.
A direct invasion is not even the most likely path toward conflict. Only 8% of the experts described an amphibious invasion within ten years as likely, while 63% called it possible and 27% unlikely. Force short of invasion received much higher probabilities, with 52% saying deliberate escalation such as a blockade was likely or very likely. An accidental military incident was considered even more dangerous, with 34% saying a collision or accident around the Taiwan Strait was likely and another 22% calling it very likely. When warships and aircraft from opposing nuclear powers continually operate around the same small body of water, war does not require some grand master plan. It requires one mistake followed by politicians who refuse to back down.
A later CSIS survey of American and Taiwanese experts reinforces that point. Roughly 90% of U.S. experts and 62% of Taiwanese experts believed China already possessed the capability to impose a law-enforcement-led quarantine that substantially reduces trade into Taiwan. Around 80% of American experts and 60% of Taiwanese experts believed Beijing could execute a PLA blockade, while Taiwanese experts were considerably more skeptical that China could successfully carry out an invasion. If Beijing wanted to coerce Taiwan during the following five years, experts considered a quarantine the most likely option. If China decided it wanted immediate unification, however, approximately 80% regarded a highly kinetic joint blockade as likely or very likely.
This is where the economic consequences become enormous because Taiwan does not need to be invaded for the world economy to be thrown into chaos. A quarantine or blockade would immediately threaten shipping, insurance, semiconductor supply chains, electronics, automobiles, communications equipment, and virtually every modern industry dependent upon advanced chips. The later CSIS survey found most American and Taiwanese experts did not believe Taiwan could withstand a Chinese blockade for longer than three months without substantial U.S. intervention. Washington would then face the decision nobody wants to discuss honestly: accept China’s blockade or attempt to break it militarily and risk direct war between two nuclear powers.
Taiwan is also the world’s semiconductor pressure point. The island’s importance to advanced chip manufacturing means a serious blockade would not remain a regional event. Factories thousands of miles away could discover that a conflict they thought had nothing to do with them suddenly prevents them from obtaining critical components. Markets would begin repricing the risk immediately, shipping premiums would explode, companies would scramble for inventory, and governments would discover once again how fragile global supply chains have become. This is why capital will react long before politicians formally declare that a war has begun.
What I find particularly revealing in the later CSIS survey is the difference between American confidence and Taiwanese confidence in Washington. An astonishing 96% of American experts were completely or moderately confident that the United States would intervene militarily if China invaded Taiwan during the following five years. Taiwanese experts were less confident in American intervention and considerably less confident that U.S. allies would join the fight. It is always easier for people thousands of miles away to be certain about somebody else’s war.
This is precisely why Taiwan remains one of the critical geopolitical pressure points as we move toward 2029. The danger is not simply that China arbitrarily decides to invade. The greater danger is escalation, miscalculation, political promises that cannot be withdrawn, and Western policymakers convincing themselves that every additional provocation somehow produces deterrence. China has made its position on formal independence perfectly clear, and even the experts inside the Western foreign-policy establishment overwhelmingly acknowledge that Beijing would react with force if that line were crossed.
If Taiwan declares formal independence, 77% of the experts surveyed believed China would invade within six months. That is not a statistic policymakers should treat as another war-game scenario. It is a warning about what happens when politicians deliberately remove the ambiguity that has helped keep the peace.

立法会议员与元朗及黄大仙区议会会面讨论发展事宜 |中国劳工公告栏
星期五, 27 十一月 2026 · 香港 香港及中国劳工新闻英文版
立法会议员与元朗及黄大仙区议会会面讨论发展事宜
香港立法会议员于11月27日与元朗和黄大仙区议会会面，讨论交通连接、防洪和重建计划等社区问题。
香港立法会议员于11月27日在立法会综合大楼与元朗及黄大仙区议会会面，就社区发展及市民关注的问题交换意见。
立法会议员与元朗区议会会面时，讨论可否配合北部新市镇的发展同步完成交通基建，以提高交通效率。其他议题包括加快元朗明渠改善工程，提升防洪能力；进一步提升天水围河岸沿线设施；加强监测及及时更换老化水管，提高供水稳定性。
会议由立法会议员何君尧召集。共有31名立法会议员出席，包括何俊英、周浩鼎、刘叶强、周少生、姚柏康、梁子英、陈沛良、陈勇、陈兆雄、陈浩民、严光、蒲国明、方秀忠、江慧娴、吴焕杰、吴英邦、李光宇、林明峰、姚祖辉、姚明、范杰强、陈祖光、陈晓峰、郭富荣、庄浩峰、刘文君、刘家强、邓明森、魏明德及谭振国。
立法会议员在与黄大仙区议会会面时，讨论在重建为政府综合大楼前，活化前彩虹道街市的部分地下空间作短期社区活动，以善用土地资源。他们亦检视黄大仙防止大规模水浸的措施，以加强雨季和极端天气的应对措施，并讨论彩虹村重建计划的文物保育、时间表和居民搬迁安排。
会议由立法会议员胡永嘉主持。共有28名立法会议员出席，包括郑子信、周兆生、林振声、姚百康、梁子英、陈勇、陈兆雄、陈启恩、黄国、杨耀忠、古浩明、邓迪嘉、刘志鹏、陈永光、方秀忠、吴应邦、李家权、林明峰、范杰强、洪锦珍、陈祖光、陈晓峰、张佩刚、黄锦良、刘家强、邓明森及魏明德。
立法会议员表示，会继续透过相关委员会反映公众意见，并跟进与区议会及政府当局讨论的事宜。

Legislators meet Yuen Long and Wong Tai Sin district councils on development | China Labour Bulletin Board
Friday, 27 Nov 2026 · Hong Kong Hong Kong and China labour news in English
Legislators meet Yuen Long and Wong Tai Sin district councils on development
Hong Kong legislators met Yuen Long and Wong Tai Sin district councils on 27 November to discuss community issues including transport links, flood prevention and redevelopment plans.
Hong Kong legislators met with the Yuen Long and Wong Tai Sin district councils at the Legislative Council Complex on 27 November to exchange views on community development and public concerns.
During the meeting with Yuen Long District Council, legislators discussed whether transport infrastructure could be completed in step with the development of the Northern New Towns to improve transport efficiency. Other topics included accelerating the improvement works on Yuen Long nullah to enhance flood prevention capacity, further upgrading facilities along the Tin Shui Wai riverfront, and strengthening monitoring and timely replacement of ageing water mains to improve water supply stability.
The meeting was convened by legislator Junius Ho Kwan-yiu. A total of 31 legislators attended, including Ho Chun-ying, Holden Chow Ho-ding, Lau Ip-keung, Chow Siu-sang, Yiu Pak-hong, Leung Tsz-ying, Chan Pui-leung, Chan Yung, Daryl Chan Siu-hung, Chan Ho-man, Yim Kong, Po Kwok-ming, Fong Sau-chung, Vivian Kong, Ng Wun-kit, Ng Ying-pong, Li Kwong-yu, Lam Ming-fung, Yiu Cho-fai, Yiu Ming, Fan Kit-keung, Chan Cho-kwong, Selina Chan Hiu-fung, Kwok Fu-wing, Chong Ho-fung, Lau Man-kwan, Lau Ka-keung, Tang Ming-sam, Ngai Ming-tak and Tam Chun-kwok.
In the meeting with Wong Tai Sin District Council, legislators discussed activating part of the underground space at the former Choi Hung Road market for short-term community activities before its redevelopment into a government complex, to make better use of land resources. They also reviewed measures to prevent large-scale flooding in Wong Tai Sin to enhance preparedness for rainy seasons and extreme weather, and discussed heritage conservation, timeline and resident relocation arrangements for the Choi Hung Estate redevelopment plan.
The meeting was convened by legislator Michael Wu Wing-ka. A total of 28 legislators attended, including Cheng Tsz-shun, Chow Siu-sang, Lam Chun-sing, Yiu Pak-hong, Leung Tsz-ying, Chan Yung, Daryl Chan Siu-hung, Star Chan Kai-yan, Wong Kwok, Yeung Yiu-chung, Ku Ho-ming, Tang Tik-ka, Lau Chi-pang, Chan Wing-kwong, Fong Sau-chung, Ng Ying-pong, Lee Ka-kuen, Lam Ming-fung, Fan Kit-keung, Hung Kam-chun, Chan Cho-kwong, Selina Chan Hiu-fung, Cheung Pui-kong, Wong Kam-leung, Lau Ka-keung, Tang Ming-sam and Ngai Ming-tak.
Legislators said they would continue to reflect public views through the relevant committees and follow up on the matters discussed with the district councils and government authorities.

香港旅游发展局推出有史以来规模最大的“冬城”圣诞节，活动范围从中环扩展到尖沙咀和铜锣湾。文化体育及旅游局局长在11月27日举行的启动仪式上表示，由于公众和游客对灯光秀的需求强劲，委员会已将中环和尖沙咀的灯光秀从当天晚上七时至六时开始。
铜锣湾的新“冬季小镇”是与房地产开发商希慎集团合作创建的，以童话精灵为主题，设有灯光秀、户外酒吧和圣诞市场。秘书表示，这将为游客提供另一个节日拍照地点。
2026年旅游数据显示强劲增长，1月至10月游客人数同比增长12%。秘书将这一增长归因于一系列重大事件。演讲称，前九个月的零售额增长约8%，至2,990亿港元，而餐饮收入增长约2%，至830亿港元。
董事会计划通过涵盖国际艺术、中国艺术和季节性庆祝活动的三部分活动来保持势头。圣诞节后，日程包括除夕倒计时和中国新年国际联欢晚会。秘书表示，董事会将继续创新，展示香港作为亚洲活动之都的形象。
秘书感谢旅游局和希慎的支持，并祝大家圣诞快乐。

Hong Kong expands Christmas 'Winter Town' to three locations, adds earlier light shows
Hong Kong's tourism board has expanded its 'Winter Town' Christmas event to include Causeway Bay for the first time, with light shows starting an hour earlier from 27 November. The Cultural and Tourism Secretary said visitor numbers rose 12 per cent in the first 10 months of 2026, boosting retail an
The Hong Kong Tourism Board has launched the largest-ever edition of its 'Winter Town' Christmas festival, expanding the event from Central to include Tsim Sha Tsui and Causeway Bay. Speaking at a launch ceremony on 27 November, Secretary for Culture, Sports and Tourism said the board had brought forward the start of light shows in Central and Tsim Sha Tsui from 7pm to 6pm from that day, citing strong public and tourist demand for the displays.
The new 'Winter Town' in Causeway Bay, created in partnership with property developer Hysan Holdings, features a fairy-elf theme with light shows, an outdoor bar and a Christmas market. The secretary said it would provide another festive photo spot for visitors.
Tourism data for 2026 showed strong growth, with visitor arrivals from January to October up 12 per cent year-on-year. The secretary attributed the increase to a series of major events. Retail sales in the first nine months rose about 8 per cent to HK$299 billion, while restaurant revenue increased about 2 per cent to HK$83 billion, according to the speech.
The board plans to sustain momentum through a three-part event line-up covering international arts, Chinese arts and seasonal festivities. After Christmas, the schedule includes New Year's Eve countdown and the Chinese New Year International Gala Night. The secretary said the board would continue to innovate to showcase Hong Kong as an Asian events capital.
The secretary thanked the tourism board and Hysan for their support, and wished everyone a happy Christmas.

香港SmartPLAY系统遭黑客攻击，9万账户受影响 |中国劳工公告栏
星期五, 27 十一月 2026 · 香港 香港及中国劳工新闻英文版
香港SmartPLAY系统遭黑客攻击 9万账户受影响
香港康乐及文化事务署表示，黑客侵入了SmartPLAY的“重新启动康体通账户”功能，导致约9万名用户的个人数据被泄露。该部门已禁用该功能，通知警方和隐私部门，并正在联系受影响的个人。
香港政府康乐及文化事务署（康文署）披露了一起影响其 SmartPLAY 系统的网络安全事件，该系统于 2023 年取代了旧的 Leisure Link 平台，允许居民预订体育设施和康乐活动。
根据2026年11月27日发布的政府声明，黑客非法访问了SmartPLAY的“重新激活康体通账户”功能。此功能旨在帮助以前的 Leisure Link 用户更快地将数据迁移到新系统。此次泄露涉及约 90,000 个康体通账户的个人数据，包括出生日期、电话号码、地址、性别和电子邮件地址。其中，约有1500名用户的名字被曝光。康文署强调，并无任何身份证明文件资料遭泄露，且SmartPLAY并无储存任何信用卡或其他付款资料。
该部门还报告称，“忘记用户 ID 或密码”功能被黑客滥用，导致系统向受影响的用户发送验证码电子邮件。康文署表示，事件不涉及个人资料盗窃。该公司建议收到此类电子邮件的用户不要忽略这些电子邮件，并指示需要更改密码的用户携带香港身份证前往指定服务站。这两项职能均已暂停，等待全面调查。
康文署表示，已责令系统承办商进行深入调查并提交报告。该公司已向警方报案，并通知保安局、数码政策办公室及个人资料私隐专员公署。该部门正在与承包商合作，通知受影响的个人，并正在审查其安全措施，寻求隐私监管机构和数字政策办公室的建议，以防止再次发生。康文署注意到连日亦有黑客非法侵入康文署城市售票网票务系统，并表示会要求警方评估该等事件是否涉及严重犯罪活动。
